name: Overdrive: Harder Than the LSAT
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer to be harder than the real test (difficulty 6), using the real test's question types and stem wording. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Director of the Orrin Choral Society: Here is what I know about all of our current members, as of this season's official roster. Everyone who sings in our chamber ensemble can sight-read music fluently. No member who joined the society after 2020 can sight-read fluently unless that member has completed the society's music theory course. Every member who has completed the theory course was recruited by me personally, though not everyone I recruited has taken it. Most of our sopranos sing in the chamber ensemble, and some of our sopranos joined after 2020. I personally recruited several of our altos and tenors, but none of our sopranos. Finally, a few members who joined before 2020 cannot sight-read fluently either, since our entrance audition did not test sight-reading at all until 2019.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the director's statements?
choices: No member of the chamber ensemble joined the society after 2020.
Most of the members who can sight-read fluently are sopranos.
Some members who joined after 2020 have completed the music theory course.
Every soprano who joined the society before 2020 sings in the chamber ensemble.
Fewer than half of the society's sopranos joined the society after 2020.
questions.explanation: No soprano was recruited by the director, so no soprano has taken the theory course, so no soprano who joined after 2020 can sight-read, so none of them is in the ensemble. Since most sopranos are in the ensemble, most sopranos did not join after 2020: fewer than half did, as (E) says. (A) is the near-miss: it's true of sopranos, but a non-soprano who joined after 2020 and took the course could sight-read and sing in the ensemble. The rest are unsupported quantity or 'every' claims.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Ensemble -> sight-reads; 2. Joined after 2020 and sight-reads -> took theory course; 3. Took course -> recruited by director; 4. Most sopranos in ensemble; some sopranos joined after 2020; 5. Director recruited no sopranos.

breakdown.analysis: Chain the sopranos through: not recruited -> no course -> (if joined after 2020) can't sight-read -> not in ensemble. So the after-2020 sopranos are all outside the ensemble. 'Most sopranos are in the ensemble' then forces the after-2020 sopranos to be a minority of sopranos. The last sentence about pre-2020 members is filler. Watch the scope: the chain works for sopranos only, because only they are known to have skipped the course.

choices.note: Near-miss on scope. True for sopranos, but nothing stops an alto who joined in 2022, was recruited by the director and took the course, from sight-reading and singing in the ensemble.
No counts of sight-readers outside the soprano section are given. Altos and tenors could make up most of them.
Possible but not supported. Every course-taker was recruited by the director, but nothing says any of them joined after 2020.
Only 'most' sopranos are in the ensemble; some pre-2020 sopranos (including the ones who can't sight-read) may sing elsewhere.

CORRECT. Sopranos who joined after 2020 can't sight-read (no soprano took the course), so none is in the ensemble. Most sopranos are in the ensemble, so the after-2020 sopranos must be fewer than half.

questions.stimulus: Festival director: Our rules interlock in ways that applicants sometimes miss, and several filmmakers have asked me this month which prizes their films can still compete for. A film is eligible for the jury prize only if it has its world premiere at our festival. No film that premieres here may be screened in the outdoor amphitheater unless it already has a distributor, because distributors cover the amphitheater's licensing fees. A film cannot both have a distributor and receive support from our emerging-filmmaker fund, and every documentary in this year's program receives support from that fund. Some critics say that these rules penalize documentaries; I disagree, since documentaries compete for an audience award that fiction films cannot win. In any case, it follows from our rules that The Salt Road, a documentary in this year's program, is not eligible for the jury prize.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the festival director's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every film screened in the outdoor amphitheater is eligible for the jury prize.
The Salt Road will have its world premiere at the festival.
The Salt Road will be screened in the festival's outdoor amphitheater.
No documentary in this year's program has a distributor.
Every film that premieres at the festival without a distributor receives support from the emerging-filmmaker fund.
questions.explanation: The Salt Road is a documentary, so it gets fund support, so it has no distributor. A premiering film without a distributor can't be screened outdoors; contrapositively, a film screened outdoors without a distributor didn't premiere here. If The Salt Road is screened outdoors (C), it didn't premiere here, so it isn't eligible for the jury prize. (B) is the trap: premiering here plus no distributor only rules out the amphitheater, and says nothing against eligibility.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Salt Road is not eligible for the jury prize.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Jury → premiere. Premiere AND amphitheater → distributor. Not both (distributor, fund). Documentary → fund. Salt Road is a documentary.

breakdown.analysis: Run the known chain: Salt Road → fund → no distributor. The conclusion needs 'no premiere' (the contrapositive of jury → premiere). Where can 'no premiere' come from? Only from the amphitheater rule: (premiere AND amphitheater) → distributor; with no distributor, NOT(premiere AND amphitheater). So if Salt Road is in the amphitheater, it can't have premiered here. The gap closes only after combining the fund rule's contrapositive with the amphitheater rule's.

choices.note: This reverses the direction we need. It sends amphitheater films TO eligibility, and we don't even know Salt Road is in the amphitheater.
Near miss. Premiere plus no distributor means Salt Road can't be screened outdoors. That's all; premiering is exactly what eligibility requires, so nothing rules it out.
CORRECT. In the amphitheater with no distributor, Salt Road can't be a film that premiered here (premiere + amphitheater would require a distributor). No premiere → not eligible for the jury prize.
Already follows from the premises (documentary → fund → no distributor). Adding it gets us no further toward 'no premiere'.
This tells us when a film gets fund support, a fact we already have for Salt Road. It produces no link to 'no premiere'.

questions.stimulus: Operations manager: Last year we installed self-order kiosks in twelve of our forty cafés, chosen by our regional managers. Over the following year, sales at those twelve cafés rose 9 percent, compared with 4 percent at the other twenty-eight. Some have suggested that the difference reflects the new seasonal menu we introduced last spring, but that menu was introduced at all forty cafés at the same time, so it cannot explain why one group outpaced the other. Admittedly, two of the twelve kiosk cafés also extended their opening hours last year; but even if those two are set aside, sales at the remaining ten rose 8 percent, still double the rate at the cafés without kiosks. The kiosks, therefore, were responsible for at least part of the faster growth in sales at the twelve cafés that received them.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the operations manager's argument?
choices: Did sales at the kiosk cafés rise more in the busiest months of the year than in the slowest months?
Before the kiosks were installed, were the twelve cafés that the regional managers selected the ones with the highest sales among the chain's forty cafés?
Have the regional managers who chose the twelve cafés since recommended installing kiosks at any of the other twenty-eight?
Before the kiosks were installed, had sales at the twelve selected cafés already been growing faster than sales at the other twenty-eight?
Was the seasonal menu introduced last spring more expensive, on average, than the menu it replaced?
questions.explanation: The kiosk cafés weren't chosen at random; managers picked them. If they were already the faster-growing cafés, the gap after installation could be just their existing trend, and the kiosks did nothing. If they weren't, the causal claim looks stronger. (D) asks exactly that. (B) is the near miss: it asks about the LEVEL of sales, not the rate of growth, and high-selling cafés needn't be growing faster.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The kiosks caused at least part of the faster sales growth at the twelve cafés.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Kiosk cafés grew 9% vs 4%; the new menu was chain-wide, so it can't explain the gap; excluding the two cafés with longer hours still leaves 8% vs 4%.

breakdown.analysis: The manager rules out two alternative causes (the menu, the longer hours) but ignores how the twelve cafés were picked. A non-random selection invites a pre-existing difference. The most useful question is whether the kiosk group was already outpacing the others. Watch for a question that sounds like it targets selection but asks about the wrong measure.

choices.note: Seasonal timing within the kiosk cafés doesn't tell us whether kiosks caused the difference between the two groups. Either answer leaves the argument as it was.
Near miss. It targets the selection but asks about the size of sales, not their growth. A café with the highest sales can grow slowly; either answer leaves the trend question open.
What the managers later recommended is opinion, not evidence of cause. Either answer leaves the argument untouched.

CORRECT. Yes: the twelve were already growing faster, so the post-installation gap could be their existing trend, which weakens the argument. No: the gap appeared only after the kiosks arrived, which strengthens it.
The menu was introduced at all forty cafés, so its price affects both groups alike and can't explain why one group outgrew the other.

questions.stimulus: Hospital administrator: Of all the patients readmitted to Brennock Hospital within thirty days of discharge last year, 62 percent were over seventy years old. In a pilot program, nurses telephoned recently discharged patients, drawn from all age groups, to review their medications, and readmissions among the patients who were called fell by nearly half. Unfortunately, we cannot afford enough nurse time to call every discharged patient, so we plan to call only those over seventy. Critics on the nursing staff object that this narrower plan will leave many preventable readmissions unprevented. But calling only patients over seventy will still prevent most of the readmissions that calling every discharged patient would prevent, and since patients over seventy make up only about a quarter of those we discharge, it will require far less nurse time.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the administrator's argument?
choices: In the pilot program, the calls reduced readmissions by about the same proportion among patients in every age group.
Nurses report that calls to patients over seventy typically take longer than calls to younger patients, because more medications must be reviewed.
Patients over seventy made up less than a third of all the patients the hospital discharged last year.
More than half of the patients who were called in the pilot program were over seventy years old.
Many of the patients over seventy who were readmitted last year had also been readmitted in earlier years.
questions.explanation: The disputed claim is that the over-seventy group holds most of the readmissions calls could prevent. That needs more than their 62 percent share of readmissions: the calls must work about as well for them. If calls cut every group's readmissions by the same proportion, 62 percent of the preventable readmissions are among the over-seventies, as (A) secures. (C) is the main trap: it restates the 'about a quarter of discharges' premise the administrator has already asserted, and that share of discharges does nothing for the disputed claim about preventable readmissions. (D) concerns who was called, not how well the calls worked.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Calling only patients over seventy will prevent most of the readmissions that calling everyone would prevent (while using far less nurse time).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 62 percent of readmissions are over seventy; calls cut readmissions by nearly half in a mixed-age pilot; over-seventies are about a quarter of discharges.

breakdown.analysis: Shares of readmissions aren't shares of preventable readmissions. If calls barely helped older patients but almost eliminated readmissions among younger ones, most preventable readmissions could be among the young despite the 62 percent figure. Prephrase: calls work at least as well for the over-seventies. The efficiency half of the conclusion is already backed by a stated premise, so an answer repeating it adds little.

choices.note: CORRECT. With equal proportional effect, the readmissions prevented in each group track each group's share of readmissions, so 62 percent of preventable readmissions fall among the over-seventies: most of them.
Irrelevant to which readmissions get prevented, and if anything it trims the claimed savings in nurse time.

Tempting, but the administrator already asserts that over-seventies are only about a quarter of discharges, so 'less than a third' adds nothing. Restating that premise doesn't touch the contested claim, which is about where the preventable readmissions are.
Says who was in the pilot, not whether the calls worked as well for older patients as for younger ones. A pilot full of older patients could still have shown its effect mainly among the young.
Repeat readmissions tell us nothing about whether calls prevent them. It doesn't bear on the comparison the plan depends on.

questions.stimulus: Historian: It is commonly said that the printing press spread literacy across sixteenth-century Europe. Yet in the regions where presses were most numerous, literacy rates rose no faster than elsewhere for nearly a century after printing arrived. Nor is this surprising, given that the overwhelming majority of early printed books were in Latin, a language read almost exclusively by people who were already educated. Early printing, then, mainly enlarged the libraries of an existing elite rather than enlarging the reading public. Admittedly, printing did eventually transform popular literacy, through the flood of cheap vernacular pamphlets that the religious controversies of the later sixteenth century produced. But the common view compresses these two phases into one, and in doing so it credits the press itself with an effect that depended on a later change in what was printed.
questions.stem: The claim that early printing mainly enlarged the libraries of an existing elite rather than enlarging the reading public plays which one of the following roles in the historian's argument?
choices: It is the argument's main conclusion, which the historian supports with evidence about literacy rates and about the language of early printed books.
It is drawn from evidence the historian presents, and it is in turn used to support the historian's claim about what the common view gets wrong.
It is a concession to the common view, which the historian then qualifies by distinguishing two phases in the history of printing.
It is a premise offered in support of an intermediate conclusion, which in turn supports the argument's main conclusion.
It is an explanation offered to reconcile the common view with the evidence about literacy rates in regions with many presses.
questions.explanation: The claim is introduced with 'then', drawn from the literacy-rate data and the Latin point, and it establishes the first, elite-only phase that the main conclusion depends on: the common view wrongly credits the press itself with an effect that came only with later vernacular printing. So it's an intermediate conclusion (B). (A) mistakes it for the main conclusion, which is the final sentence. (D) is the near miss: it treats the claim as an unsupported premise, but the claim is itself supported.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The common view credits the press itself with an effect that depended on a later change in what was printed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Literacy didn't rise faster where presses were numerous; early books were in Latin → (intermediate) early printing served an existing elite. Concession: printing eventually transformed literacy via vernacular pamphlets.

breakdown.analysis: Find the main conclusion first: it's the last sentence, a rebuttal of the opening view. Then trace the claim in question: 'then' signals it's drawn from the two preceding facts, and it supplies the first phase of the 'two phases' the conclusion relies on. Supported and supporting = intermediate conclusion. Don't confuse it with the 'Admittedly' sentence, which is the concession.

choices.note: The main conclusion is the final sentence, about what the common view gets wrong. This claim feeds that conclusion rather than being it.
CORRECT. It follows ('then') from the literacy data and the Latin point, and it establishes the elite-only first phase that grounds the final claim that the common view misattributes the effect.
That describes the 'Admittedly' sentence about vernacular pamphlets. The claim in question opposes the common view rather than conceding anything to it.
Near miss. It treats the claim as a bare premise, but the claim is itself drawn from evidence. It is the intermediate conclusion, not a premise supporting one.
The claim doesn't reconcile the common view with the data; it uses the data against the common view.

questions.stimulus: After the Fennick restaurant chain began printing calorie counts beside every item on its menus, the share of main courses ordered that contained under 600 calories rose from 30 percent to 45 percent. Public health researchers who had urged the change expected the average number of calories per customer to fall. Instead, it rose slightly. The chain changed none of its recipes or portion sizes during this period, its prices stayed the same, and the average number of items each customer ordered did not change. Nor were the calorie counts misleading: an independent laboratory found them accurate to within 3 percent. The researchers have therefore been left trying to understand how customers who were evidently paying attention to calorie counts could have ended up eating more calories per visit than before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many customers who switched to a lower-calorie main course ordered a rich dessert in place of the salad or steamed vegetables they would otherwise have ordered as a side.
The number of customers the chain served each week rose after the calorie counts began to appear on its menus.
Before the calorie counts appeared, most of the chain's customers had underestimated the calories in its main courses.
Customers who had ordered main courses with under 600 calories before the change continued to order them afterward.
The lower-calorie main courses whose sales rose the most were among the most expensive main courses on the menu.
questions.explanation: With recipes, portions and the number of items per customer all fixed, calories per customer can rise only if the mix of items shifted toward higher-calorie ones somewhere. (A) supplies that shift: the calories saved on the main course were more than spent on a dessert that replaced a light side. (B) is the rate-versus-total trap: more customers raises total calories, not calories per customer. (C) explains why customers switched, not why calories rose, and (D) and (E) leave the per-customer figure unexplained.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Customers shifted toward lower-calorie main courses, yet average calories per customer rose, with recipes, portions, prices and items ordered unchanged.

breakdown.analysis: The stimulus blocks the easy exits: no recipe changes, no bigger portions, no extra items, no inaccurate counts. What's left is substitution among items. If people ordered the same number of items, some item other than the main course must have become higher-calorie on average. Look for a trade inside the order: light main course, heavy something else.

choices.note: CORRECT. The number of items stays the same (a dessert replaces a side), but the swap from a light side to a rich dessert can more than cancel the calories saved on the main course. That's how attentive customers end up eating more.
Trap. More customers means more total calories served, but the puzzle is about the average per customer, which a bigger headcount can't move.
This explains why the labels changed behavior, pushing people toward lighter main courses. It doesn't explain why their total calories went up.
Consistent with the facts but no help: these customers' orders didn't change, so they can't account for the rise.
Prices are irrelevant here, and the chain's prices didn't change. Which lighter dishes sold best doesn't explain more calories.

questions.stimulus: Zoning official: The zoning board grants a variance to a business only if the city's traffic office has reviewed the business's proposal, and the traffic office reviews no proposal except one that includes an acceptable parking plan. A parking plan is acceptable only if the business either owns an off-street lot or holds a shared-use agreement with a neighboring property. In the Mill District, moreover, no business may hold a shared-use agreement unless it has operated at its current location for at least five years. The Ostrander Bakery, which is in the Mill District, owns no off-street lot. Ostrander's owners argue that the bakery's popularity with commuters justifies special consideration, but popularity is not among the criteria the board is permitted to weigh. Therefore, Ostrander will not be granted a variance.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the zoning official's conclusion to be properly drawn?
choices: Every business in the Mill District that has operated at its current location for at least five years owns an off-street lot.
Every business in the Mill District that owns an off-street lot has operated at its current location for at least five years.
Ostrander holds no shared-use agreement with any property located outside the Mill District.
The traffic office has never reviewed a proposal submitted by a business in the Mill District.
The zoning board grants variances only to businesses that have operated at their current locations for at least five years.
questions.explanation: Variance → traffic review → acceptable plan → (lot OR shared-use). Ostrander has no lot, so it needs a shared-use agreement, which in the Mill District requires five years at its location. (A) says five-year Mill District businesses own lots; Ostrander has no lot, so by contrapositive it hasn't been there five years, so it can't hold a shared-use agreement, so no acceptable plan, no review, no variance. (B) is the reversed version and proves nothing about Ostrander.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ostrander will not be granted a variance.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Variance → reviewed → acceptable plan → (lot OR shared-use). Mill District: shared-use → ≥5 years. Ostrander: Mill District, no lot.

breakdown.analysis: Work backward: to deny the variance we need 'no acceptable plan', i.e., no lot AND no shared-use agreement. We have no lot. We need no shared-use agreement, which follows if Ostrander has been at its location under five years. The stimulus doesn't say how long. The key must give us that, and it can do so obliquely: a rule whose contrapositive, applied to 'no lot', yields 'under five years'.

choices.note: CORRECT. Contrapositive: a Mill District business without a lot hasn't operated there five years. Ostrander has no lot, so it's under five years, so it can't hold a shared-use agreement, so it has no acceptable plan, no traffic review, and no variance.
The reversal. It runs from 'lot' to 'five years', but Ostrander has no lot, so this rule tells us nothing about it.
Near miss. This rules out agreements with properties outside the district, but Ostrander could still hold one with a neighbor inside the district.
'Has never' reviewed is about the past. It doesn't guarantee the office won't review Ostrander's proposal.
This adds a new requirement but we still don't know how long Ostrander has operated, so we can't tell whether it fails it.

questions.stimulus: Historian: For a century, scholars have credited the shipwright Anneke Vos with designing the narrow-hulled trading vessel that dominated Baltic commerce after 1640. The attribution has always rested on a single document: a letter, dated 1652, in which a merchant praises "Vos's hull" and records its dimensions. But analysis of the letter's paper and ink shows that it was written no earlier than 1720, decades after Vos's death, by someone who could have known of her work only by report. Defenders of the attribution suggest that the document might be a faithful copy of a genuine 1652 letter, yet it refers in passing to a trade treaty signed in 1715, a reference that no faithful copy of a 1652 letter could contain. With its only documentary support discredited, the attribution must be rejected: Vos did not design the vessel, and the credit for its design belongs elsewhere.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the historian's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: treats the absence of any evidence that the document is a copy as proof that it is not a copy
relies on an analysis of the document's paper and ink without establishing that such analysis can reliably date a document
takes for granted that a document bearing a false date must have been produced with the intention of deceiving its readers
rejects a hypothesis about the document's origin solely because that hypothesis was advanced by defenders of the attribution
takes the discrediting of the only evidence that has been offered for a claim to establish that the claim is false
questions.explanation: The historian shows, convincingly, that the only evidence for Vos's authorship is worthless. That leaves the attribution unsupported, not refuted, yet the historian concludes that Vos did NOT design the vessel. (E) names that leap. (A) is the trap: the historian does reject the copy hypothesis, but on positive evidence (the 1715 treaty reference), not merely for lack of evidence.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Vos did not design the vessel (so the attribution must be rejected).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The only evidence is a letter dated 1652; the letter was really written after 1720 by someone relying on report; it can't be a faithful copy because it mentions a 1715 treaty.

breakdown.analysis: Everything up to 'With its only documentary support discredited' is well argued. The jump is in the last clause: from 'this evidence fails' to 'the claim is false'. Lack of support is not proof of the opposite; Vos may still have designed the vessel. The other flaw-sounding moves (dating the letter, rejecting the copy theory) are each backed by evidence.

choices.note: Near miss. The historian does reject the copy theory, but not for lack of evidence: the 1715 treaty reference is positive evidence that the document can't be a faithful copy of a 1652 letter.
The dating is independently confirmed by the treaty reference, and nothing suggests the analysis is unreliable. This isn't where the argument goes wrong.
The historian never says the writer meant to deceive; the argument needs only that the letter wasn't written in 1652 by a firsthand witness.
The copy theory is rejected because of the 1715 reference, not because of who proposed it.
CORRECT. Showing that the only evidence for a claim is unreliable leaves the claim unsupported, not false. The historian moves from 'the letter proves nothing' to 'Vos did not design the vessel.'

questions.stimulus: Biologist: In the decade after feral cats were first recorded on Corran Island, the island's breeding population of sand plovers fell by 60 percent. Many conservationists blame the cats, but the evidence, on closer inspection, points elsewhere. Nearly all of Corran's plover nests lie on the open dunes of the northern shore, and over three breeding seasons, motion-triggered cameras placed at forty of those nests recorded cats approaching only two, neither of which was disturbed. Moreover, the plover population of nearby Lusk Island, which has never had cats, declined just as steeply over the same decade. Whatever is driving the decline, then, it is not the cats; it must be some factor that the two islands share, such as the dwindling supply of the shoreline insects on which plover chicks feed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the biologist's argument?
choices: Shoreline insect populations on Corran Island have not declined noticeably over the past decade.
Camera surveys of nesting shorebirds on other islands have sometimes failed to record predators that were known to be present nearby.
Most of Lusk Island's plovers spend the winter in the inland marshes of Corran Island, where the feral cats chiefly hunt.
The feral cats on Corran Island feed mainly on rabbits, which are abundant there throughout the year.
Some of the plover nests on Corran Island are located away from the dunes of the northern shore.
questions.explanation: The biologist rests on two pieces of evidence: cameras at nests saw almost no cat activity, and cat-free Lusk declined just as much. (C) undercuts both at once: if Lusk's plovers winter in Corran's marshes, where the cats hunt, then cats could be killing adults away from the nests the cameras watched, and Lusk's 'cat-free' population is exposed to the same cats. (A) is the main trap: it attacks only the example the biologist offered ('such as'), not the claim that the cause is not the cats. (B) is about other islands, and (E) is already conceded by 'nearly all'.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The cats are not causing the plover decline; it must be a factor common to Corran and Lusk.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Cameras at 40 nests on Corran saw cats approach only two, with no disturbance; cat-free Lusk declined just as steeply.

breakdown.analysis: Both premises quietly assume that cats could only hurt plovers at the nests, and that Lusk's birds never meet cats. Prephrase: the cats kill plovers somewhere the cameras weren't looking, and Lusk's birds go there too. Watch for answers that attack the biologist's illustrative example (insects) rather than the conclusion, and for answers about other places or about a few exceptional nests.

choices.note: Tempting, because it knocks out the biologist's named alternative. But the insects were offered only as an example ('such as'). The conclusion that the cats are not responsible survives intact.
Scope near-miss. Unreliable cameras elsewhere say little about these forty cameras, and 'sometimes' is weak. Even granting it, the Lusk comparison is untouched.

CORRECT. Plovers can die away from their nests, so cameras at nests miss marsh predation. And if Lusk's birds winter among Corran's cats, Lusk is not a cat-free control: the matching decline is just what cat predation would predict.
If anything this helps the biologist: the cats have plenty of other food.
The biologist already conceded this with 'nearly all.' A few nests elsewhere do not show the cats caused a 60 percent decline.

questions.stimulus: On Monday the Velde Bakery baked only two kinds of bread, rye and spelt, and by the end of the day every loaf it had baked had been either sold or donated. More than half of all the loaves baked on Monday were sold before noon, although fewer than one-third of the rye loaves were. The bakery donates a loaf only if it remains unsold at closing, and on Monday it donated exactly twelve loaves, all of them spelt. According to the manager, rye sold briskly in the afternoon: every rye loaf that had not been sold before noon was sold before closing. The manager also noted that the bakery baked more rye loaves on Monday than on any previous day, because a nearby restaurant had placed a large standing order that it collects in the afternoon.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: More than half of the loaves the bakery baked on Monday were rye.
Most of the loaves sold on Monday afternoon were rye.
Fewer than half of Monday's spelt loaves were sold before noon.
Some of Monday's spelt loaves were sold in the afternoon.
Fewer spelt loaves than rye loaves were sold on Monday afternoon.
questions.explanation: If fewer than half of the spelt loaves and fewer than a third (so fewer than half) of the rye loaves sold before noon, then fewer than half of all loaves sold before noon, contradicting the stated fact. So (C) cannot be true. (A) is the main trap: a rye majority feels incompatible with a morning dominated by spelt, but it works, for example with 60 rye and 50 spelt loaves (19 rye and 37 spelt sold before noon, 12 spelt donated, 1 spelt and 41 rye sold in the afternoon), which also makes (B), (D) and (E) true.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Only rye and spelt; every loaf sold or donated; 2. More than half of all loaves sold before noon; 3. Fewer than one-third of rye loaves sold before noon; 4. Exactly 12 loaves donated, all spelt; 5. All rye not sold before noon sold in the afternoon.

breakdown.analysis: Think averages. The before-noon share of all loaves is a weighted average of the rye share and the spelt share. If the overall share tops one-half while rye's share is under one-third, spelt's share must be over one-half. Anything denying that is impossible. Test the others with a concrete case: 60 rye, 50 spelt works (19 rye + 37 spelt = 56 of 110 before noon).

choices.note: Possible. With 60 rye and 50 spelt: 19 rye and 37 spelt sold before noon (56 of 110, more than half), 12 spelt donated, 1 spelt and 41 rye sold later.
Possible. In the same case, 41 of the 42 afternoon sales are rye.

CORRECT. Rye's before-noon share is under one-third; if spelt's were also under one-half, the combined share would be under one-half, contradicting 'more than half of all the loaves were sold before noon.'
Possible. In the 60/50 case, one spelt loaf sold in the afternoon.
Possible, and in fact likely, since every unsold rye loaf went in the afternoon. In the 60/50 case it's 1 spelt vs. 41 rye.

questions.stimulus: Every grant proposal that the Linden Foundation funds must first be reviewed by at least two outside experts, and the foundation sends a proposal to outside experts only after its treasurer has approved the proposal's budget. The treasurer, in turn, approves a budget only if it includes an independent audit plan or the applicant has received Linden funding in the past. The Sorel Institute's current proposal contains no independent audit plan, and although the institute has applied to the foundation three times before, none of those applications was funded. The institute's director has complained that the audit requirement places an unfair burden on small organizations, but however that complaint is resolved, the conclusion for this funding cycle is clear: the Linden Foundation will not fund the Sorel Institute's current proposal.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Ferrin will not be made head chef this year. Ferrin has neither completed the pastry certification nor worked at the restaurant for five years, and the owner endorses a cook only if the cook has done at least one of those things. Moreover, no one is made head chef without first managing a kitchen shift, and no one manages a shift without the owner's endorsement.

Every novel the Brisk Prize shortlists must first be nominated by two judges, and judges nominate only books that publishers have submitted by March. A publisher submits a book by March only if its author has an agent or has won a prize before. The author of Tova's novel has no agent. So Tova's novel will not be shortlisted for the Brisk Prize.

Any applicant whose references are verified is interviewed, and any applicant who is interviewed is offered a position, provided the applicant has either a degree or five years of experience. Ilya's references have been verified, and Ilya has a degree. So Ilya will be offered a position, whatever the hiring committee's other preferences.

A building is approved for occupancy only if it passes inspection, and it passes inspection only if it has either sprinklers or fire-rated doors throughout. The Ames building has sprinklers throughout, and its owners have filed every required form. So the Ames building will be approved for occupancy once its inspection is complete.

Most films the festival screens are first recommended by a programmer, and programmers recommend only films that were submitted before the deadline or made by past winners. Daro's film was submitted after the deadline, and Daro has never won. So the festival will almost certainly not screen Daro's film this year, despite its strong reviews.
questions.explanation: The argument chains necessary conditions (funded -> reviewed -> budget approved -> audit plan or past funding), denies both disjuncts at the end, and validly concludes the first condition fails. (A) does the same (head chef -> managed shift -> endorsement -> certification or five years; neither holds), just stated conclusion-first with the rules after the facts. (B) is the near-miss: it denies only one disjunct (no agent) and leaves open that the author won a prize, so its conclusion doesn't follow. (C) reasons forward to a positive conclusion, (D) treats a necessary condition as sufficient, and (E) runs on 'most', giving only a probable conclusion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match: A requires B, B requires C, C requires (D or E); neither D nor E holds; so not A. Valid, with a disjunctive last link denied on both sides.

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the skeleton: a three-link chain of 'only if' conditions ending in an 'or', both alternatives denied, so the first item fails. Then check each choice for (1) all links being necessary conditions, (2) both disjuncts denied, (3) a certain, negative conclusion. Don't be put off by order: the correct answer states its conclusion first and its facts before its rules.

choices.note: CORRECT. Head chef -> managed a shift -> owner's endorsement -> certification or five years. Ferrin has neither, so no endorsement, no shift, no promotion. Same valid chain, reordered.
Near-miss. The structure matches until the last step, where only one alternative is denied: the author might have won a prize before, so the book could still be submitted and nominated.
Valid, but it runs forward through sufficient conditions to a positive conclusion. The original denies a necessary condition to reach a negative one.
Flawed: passing inspection is necessary for approval, and sprinklers satisfy a necessary condition for passing, but neither guarantees approval.
Built on 'most', so its first link isn't a strict requirement and its conclusion is only probable ('almost certainly'). The original's chain is airtight.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Song sparrows in large cities sing at a higher minimum pitch than song sparrows in the countryside, and some researchers have concluded that urban populations have evolved this trait as an inherited adaptation to low-pitched traffic noise. A recent experiment tells against that view. Nestlings taken from city nests and raised in quiet aviaries by rural foster parents developed songs indistinguishable in pitch from those of their foster parents. Meanwhile, nestlings taken from rural nests and raised in the same aviaries by city foster parents came to sing at the higher pitch typical of city birds. In every case, then, a bird's song matched the songs of the adults it grew up hearing rather than those of its biological parents. The pitch difference between city and country sparrows is therefore a learned tradition, passed from adults to young, and not an inherited adaptation.
questions.stem: The ecologist's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choices: Song sparrows living in the wild ordinarily learn their songs from adults other than their biological parents, such as neighboring territorial males.
Had city song sparrows inherited a tendency to sing at a higher pitch, that tendency would have been evident in birds raised in quiet surroundings.
The nestlings taken from city nests came from several different city populations rather than from a single one.
No genetic factor has any influence on the pitch at which song sparrows sing.
Traffic noise in cities is generally lower in pitch than the songs of song sparrows in the countryside.
questions.explanation: The key evidence against inheritance is that city-born birds raised in QUIET aviaries sang low. That counts against an inherited tendency only if such a tendency would show itself in quiet conditions. If an inherited trait were triggered only by noise, the experiment couldn't detect it, and 'not an inherited adaptation' would be unsupported. (D) is the near miss: the argument is about the city–country difference, not every genetic influence on pitch.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The city–country pitch difference is a learned tradition, not an inherited adaptation.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Cross-fostering in quiet aviaries: city-born birds raised by rural parents sang low; rural-born birds raised by city parents sang high.

breakdown.analysis: The experiment shows learning can produce the difference. To get 'and NOT inherited', the ecologist needs the city-born birds' low songs to be a fair test of inheritance. But they were raised in quiet. If an inherited adaptation to noise only switched on in noise, quiet aviaries would hide it. Prephrase: an inherited tendency, if there were one, would have appeared in the quiet aviaries.

choices.note: Not needed; the experiment controls who the birds hear. Negated (wild birds usually learn from their parents), learning can still explain the difference.

CORRECT. Negate it: an inherited high-pitch tendency wouldn't show in quiet surroundings. Then the city-born birds' low songs say nothing against inheritance, and the conclusion that the difference is not inherited loses its support.
Sample diversity isn't required. Negated (all came from one city), the results still show song matching the rearing adults.
Near miss, too strong. The argument concerns the difference between city and country birds. Genetics could shape every sparrow's basic pitch range without explaining that difference.
This is what the rival researchers rely on, not the ecologist. Negated, the ecologist's case against inheritance is unaffected.

questions.stimulus: Arts columnist: The organizers of this summer's chamber music festival, who feuded publicly with the conservatory's faculty last year, insist that none of the performers they have hired holds a teaching position at the conservatory. The point matters, since the festival's main sponsor has made its support conditional on the festival's independence from the conservatory. That claim cannot be true. The festival has booked the Fenwick Quartet to open its season, and every member of the Fenwick Quartet completed advanced training at the conservatory. Moreover, according to the conservatory's own published figures, most people who complete advanced training there go on to hold teaching positions at the conservatory, at least part-time. So at least one member of the Fenwick Quartet must hold a teaching position at the conservatory, and the organizers' claim is false.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the arts columnist's argument?
choices: Most of the paintings in the Ashby bequest are landscapes, and every landscape in the bequest was painted before 1900. So at least some of the paintings in the Ashby bequest were painted before 1900.

At least one of the ash trees on Corbin Avenue must be infested with borers. After all, most of the trees in the city's northern wards are infested with borers, and every ash tree on Corbin Avenue stands in one of the northern wards.

Some of the firm's summer interns are law students, and most law students in the region plan to practice in the region after graduating. Therefore, at least one of the firm's summer interns plans to practice in the region.

Most of the senators who voted for the bill represent rural states, and most of the senators who voted for the bill face reelection this year. So at least one senator who represents a rural state and voted for the bill faces reelection this year.
Every member of the rowing team lives in Hale Hall, and most residents of Hale Hall are first-year students. So most first-year students at the college are members of the rowing team.
questions.explanation: The columnist reasons: all A (quartet members) are B (advanced trainees); most B teach at the conservatory; so some A teach there. That's invalid: the quartet could fall entirely within the minority of trainees who don't teach. (B) has the same structure with the conclusion moved to the front: all Corbin ashes are northern-ward trees; most northern-ward trees are infested; so some Corbin ash is infested. (C) is the near miss: same flaw, but its first premise is 'some', not 'every'.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the flaw: All A are B; most B are C; therefore at least one A is C.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: At least one Fenwick member teaches at the conservatory (so the organizers' claim is false).

breakdown.analysis: Strip it down: All A are B. Most B are C. So some A are C. A small group inside a large one can sit wholly in the minority. Now look for the same skeleton, remembering that the key may lead with its conclusion. Check each choice's quantifiers exactly; 'most + most' about the SAME group (D) and 'most + all' (A) are valid.

choices.note: Valid: most paintings are landscapes and all landscapes predate 1900, so most (hence some) paintings predate 1900. A valid argument can't match a flawed one.

CORRECT. Conclusion first, then the premises in reverse order: every Corbin ash is a northern-ward tree (all A are B), most northern-ward trees are infested (most B are C), so some Corbin ash is infested. The Corbin ashes might all be among the uninfested minority, the same flaw.
Near miss. The flaw is similar, but the first premise is 'some interns are law students', not 'every'. The columnist's argument says every member is a trainee, and (B) matches that exactly.
Valid: two 'most' statements about the same group (senators who voted for the bill) must overlap, so at least one senator is in both.
Flawed, but differently: it reverses a relationship to conclude that most first-year students row. The columnist concludes 'at least one', not a reversed 'most'.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Tarsland is divided into four regions, and every new electric bicycle sold in the country is sold in exactly one of them. Last year, manufacturers competing for a fast-growing market cut prices aggressively, and in each of the four regions the average price paid for a new electric bicycle was lower than it had been the year before. The number of new electric bicycles sold also rose in every region. Yet the average price paid for a new electric bicycle in Tarsland taken as a whole was higher last year than the year before. Some commentators have concluded that the national figure must be in error, but the agency that publishes it calculates it from exactly the same sales records that are used to calculate the four regional figures.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The region in which electric bicycles are cheapest had the largest percentage increase in the number of new electric bicycles sold.
The average price fell by a smaller percentage in the region where electric bicycles are most expensive than in any of the other three regions.
Total spending on new electric bicycles in Tarsland was higher last year than it was the year before.
Several manufacturers introduced expensive premium models last year, and those models sold well in each of the four regions.
Most of last year's sales growth came in a region where prices, though lower than before, remained far above those in the other three.
questions.explanation: A national average is a weighted average of the regional ones, so it can rise while every regional average falls if the weights shift toward the high-price region. (E) gives exactly that shift. (B) is the main trap: a smaller drop in the expensive region is still a drop, and without more weight on that region the national average can't rise. (A) shifts weight the wrong way, (C) confuses total spending with the average price, and (D) describes something already reflected in the falling regional averages.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Average price fell in every one of the four regions, yet the national average price, computed from the same records, rose.

breakdown.analysis: When every part goes down but the whole goes up, think mix. The national figure weights each region by its share of sales. If sales growth was concentrated in the expensive region, its weight rose, pulling the national average up even though each regional average fell. Look for an answer that shifts sales toward high-price regions, and beware answers about totals or about the size of the price cuts.

choices.note: Reversed. More weight on the cheapest region would push the national average down, deepening the puzzle.
Near-miss. It's still a fall in that region's price; a smaller fall can't lift the national average unless that region's share of sales grows, which this doesn't say.
Total spending would rise anyway with more bicycles sold. A total isn't an average, so this leaves the puzzle untouched.
Whatever these models did, the average in every region still fell. Since they sold well everywhere, they don't shift the regional mix, which is what's needed.

CORRECT. Growth concentrated in the high-price region raises that region's share of all sales. Since its prices remain far above the others', the national average can rise even though every regional average fell.

questions.stimulus: Planning commissioner: Under the city's heritage ordinance, a building may be demolished only if the heritage board has found that it lacks architectural significance and only if its owner has first offered it for sale to a recognized preservation trust for at least ninety days. Last March the owner of the Marlowe Warehouse offered the building to the Civic Preservation Trust, which kept the offer under review until it formally declined in August. And last month the heritage board, after hearing from three architectural historians, unanimously found that the warehouse lacks architectural significance. The developers who hope to replace the warehouse complain that the ordinance exists mainly to delay construction, while neighborhood opponents complain that the apartments planned for the site would be too tall. Neither complaint bears on the question at hand. Each of the two requirements the ordinance imposes has now been satisfied, so the Marlowe Warehouse may lawfully be demolished.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the planning commissioner's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: treats requirements that must be met for an action to be permitted as though meeting them were enough to make that action permitted
dismisses the opponents' objection to the planned apartments without showing that the objection is mistaken
relies on the heritage board's finding without establishing that the architectural historians who testified before it were qualified
infers that the owner's offer met the ordinance's ninety-day requirement merely from the fact that the trust eventually declined it
takes for granted that the heritage board's finding that a building lacks architectural significance is by itself enough to permit the building's demolition
questions.explanation: The ordinance says demolition is permitted ONLY IF two conditions hold, so they're necessary, not sufficient. Showing both are met doesn't show demolition is permitted; some other requirement or law could still forbid it. (A) says this in general terms. (E) is the trap: it's the same confusion applied to only one condition, but the argument relies on both conditions together, not on the board's finding alone.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Marlowe Warehouse may lawfully be demolished.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Demolish → (board finds no significance) AND (offered to a trust ≥ 90 days). Both conditions are met (offer March–August; board finding last month). Two complaints are set aside as irrelevant.

breakdown.analysis: 'Only if' introduces necessary conditions. The commissioner shows both necessary conditions are met and concludes the outcome is permitted, reading 'only if' as 'if'. The complaints are noise: neither concerns whether demolition is lawful. Expect the key in abstract form ('requirements…as though meeting them were enough').

choices.note: CORRECT. Each condition is introduced by 'only if', so each is required for demolition. Meeting required conditions doesn't guarantee permission, yet the commissioner concludes demolition is lawful just because they're met.
The opponents object to the apartments' height, which has nothing to do with whether the warehouse may be demolished. Setting aside an irrelevant objection isn't a flaw.
The ordinance requires that the board has made the finding, not that the finding is well founded. The historians' qualifications don't affect whether that requirement is met.
The argument doesn't rest on the trust's declining. It gives the dates: the offer stood from March until August, well over ninety days.
Near miss. This is the right kind of error attached to the wrong scope. The commissioner relies on both conditions together, not on the board's finding alone.

questions.stimulus: Sleep researcher: Last year, eleven of the Ridgeway region's twenty school districts moved their high school start times from 7:30 to 8:40 a.m., as part of a regional reform that also placed those eleven districts' school buses under a newly created transport authority. In those eleven districts, first-period absences fell by about a third, while in the other nine districts they did not change. Some skeptics have argued that students given a later start simply stay up later, so that they get no more sleep than before. But sleep logs kept by a sample of students in the eleven districts showed an average gain of forty minutes of sleep per school night. Clearly, then, it was the later start times that reduced first-period absences, by allowing students to get more sleep.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the sleep researcher's argument?
choices: Students in the nine districts that kept the 7:30 start also reported getting slightly more sleep last year than the year before.
Buses run by the new transport authority arrive at schools about as punctually as the buses that serve the nine districts that kept the 7:30 start.
Before the reform, first-period absences had been higher in the eleven districts than in the other nine.
Four of the nine districts that kept the 7:30 start also placed their school buses under the new transport authority last year.
In the eleven districts, the students whose sleep increased the most were no less likely than other students to be absent from first period.
questions.explanation: The stimulus itself names a rival cause: the same reform moved the eleven districts' buses to a new transport authority, which could have cut absences by making buses more reliable. (D) shows four districts got the new buses without the later start and saw no fall in absences (all nine were unchanged), isolating the start time. (B) is the near-miss: it compares the new buses with the wrong group's buses, so it says nothing about whether the eleven districts' own bus service improved. (C) raises a regression worry and (E) undercuts the sleep mechanism.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Later start times reduced first-period absences by giving students more sleep.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Eleven districts moved to 8:40 and absences fell by a third; nine unchanged districts saw no change; sleep logs show 40 more minutes of sleep.

breakdown.analysis: The researcher answers the skeptics' objection about sleep, but never addresses the other change buried in the first sentence: new bus management in exactly the same eleven districts. Prephrase: something that separates the start-time change from the bus change. A district that got the new buses but kept 7:30 would be the perfect control.

choices.note: If anything this weakens: sleep rose where absences didn't fall, which loosens the link between sleep and attendance.

Near-miss, and the main trap. To rule out the bus explanation you need to know whether the eleven districts' buses got better than they used to be. Matching the nine districts' buses tells you nothing about that change.
This suggests the eleven districts had unusually high absences that might have fallen back on their own. It weakens if anything.

CORRECT. These four districts got the new transport authority without the later start, and since all nine 7:30 districts saw no change in absences, the new buses alone did nothing. That leaves the start time as the cause.
This weakens the claimed mechanism: if more sleep went with no fewer absences, the absences may have fallen for some other reason.

questions.stimulus: Under the municipal code of Varrow, a building may receive a heritage tax credit only if it is listed on the city's historic register. No building is listed on the register unless it is at least seventy-five years old and has retained its original facade. Any building in the Harbor District that has retained its original facade is subject to annual structural inspection. A building subject to annual structural inspection cannot be issued a demolition permit unless the city council has voted to approve the demolition. Buildings in the Harbor District that are less than seventy-five years old are exempt from the district's height limit, and any building whose facade has been altered must display a plaque recording the alteration. The Carrow Building, which stands in the Harbor District, received a heritage tax credit this year.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: If the city council votes to approve demolishing the Carrow Building, the building can be issued a demolition permit.
Every building in the Harbor District that is at least seventy-five years old is subject to annual structural inspection.
No building outside the Harbor District that has received a heritage tax credit is subject to annual structural inspection.
The Carrow Building cannot be issued a demolition permit unless the city council has voted to approve its demolition.
Any building listed on the city's historic register is subject to annual structural inspection.
questions.explanation: Credit -> listed -> original facade (and 75+ years). Combine 'original facade' with the separate fact that Carrow is in the Harbor District, and Carrow is subject to annual inspection; so no demolition permit without council approval, as (D) says. (A) is the main trap: council approval is necessary for a permit, not sufficient. (B) drops the facade requirement, (E) drops the Harbor District requirement, and (C) asserts something the rules never address.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Credit -> listed; 2. Listed -> 75+ years and original facade; 3. Harbor District + original facade -> annual inspection; 4. Annual inspection -> no demolition permit unless council approves; 5. Carrow is in the Harbor District and got a credit. (Height-limit and plaque rules are distractors.)

breakdown.analysis: Run Carrow down the chain: credit, so listed; listed, so original facade. The chain stalls there until you bring in the location fact: Harbor District plus original facade triggers annual inspection, which triggers the council-approval requirement. The answer needs both the chain and the separate location fact. Watch 'unless' (it marks a necessary condition) and the two distractor rules.

choices.note: Reverses the condition. 'Cannot be issued a permit unless the council approves' makes approval necessary, not sufficient; other requirements could still block a permit.
Drops the facade condition. An old Harbor District building with an altered facade needn't be inspected.
The rules say what triggers inspection inside the Harbor District; they never say nothing else can trigger it elsewhere.

CORRECT. Credit -> listed -> original facade; with its Harbor District location, that makes Carrow subject to annual inspection, and inspected buildings get demolition permits only with council approval.
Drops the location condition. A listed building outside the Harbor District has an original facade but isn't covered by the inspection rule.

questions.stimulus: Policy analyst: Four years ago the county began requiring restaurants to display their health-inspection grades at their entrances. Since then the proportion of county restaurants receiving an A grade has risen from 52 percent to 79 percent. Critics contend that the rise reflects inspectors' growing reluctance to post a visible mark of failure on a restaurant's door, not any real change in restaurant kitchens. But over the same four years, the number of foodborne-illness cases that the county health department traced to restaurants fell by about a third, even though the county's population and its number of restaurants both grew slightly. Inspectors' leniency could not have produced that decline. So the critics are wrong to dismiss the rise in A grades entirely: at least part of it reflects a genuine improvement in restaurant hygiene.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the policy analyst's argument?
choices: Inspectors were not at all more reluctant to assign low grades after the display requirement took effect than they had been before.
The proportion of county restaurants receiving an A grade will continue to rise for the next several years.
Most foodborne illnesses contracted in the county are contracted at restaurants rather than at home.
Restaurants that received A grades had fewer traced illness cases than restaurants with lower grades, both before and after the requirement.
The health department did not become substantially less successful at tracing foodborne illnesses to the restaurants where they originated.
questions.explanation: The analyst's only evidence of real improvement is a drop in illness cases TRACED to restaurants. A drop in traced cases reflects cleaner kitchens only if tracing didn't get worse; if the department simply traced fewer cases, the drop is an artifact. Negate (E) and the evidence evaporates. (A) is the trap: the analyst concludes only that PART of the rise is genuine, so some added leniency is compatible with the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: At least part of the rise in A grades reflects genuine hygiene improvement.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Traced illness cases fell by a third while population and restaurant numbers grew; leniency can't explain fewer illnesses.

breakdown.analysis: Notice the measure: cases 'that the county health department traced to restaurants'. Fewer traced cases can mean fewer illnesses or worse tracing. The analyst assumes the former. Also note the hedged conclusion ('at least part', 'entirely'): any answer requiring zero leniency is too strong.

choices.note: Near miss, too strong ('not at all'). The conclusion allows leniency to explain some of the rise. Negated (inspectors grew somewhat more lenient), the argument stands.
Future grades are irrelevant. Negated (the proportion levels off), the past evidence is untouched.
Not required. Even if most illnesses come from home cooking, a one-third fall in restaurant-traced cases still bears on restaurant hygiene.
This would strengthen the link between grades and safety, but the argument doesn't need it. Negated, a county-wide fall in traced cases still suggests better hygiene.

CORRECT. Negate it: the department got much worse at tracing illnesses to restaurants. Then the drop in traced cases could reflect weaker detection rather than cleaner kitchens, and the analyst has no evidence of genuine improvement.

questions.stimulus: Retail analyst: In March, hoping to win back price-conscious shoppers, the Pellmore grocery chain began offering a free membership card that gives cardholders 5 percent off every purchase. Over the following six months, Pellmore's total sales were 9 percent higher than in the same six months a year earlier, while sales at Dunmore, its chief competitor in the same towns, fell 4 percent. Pellmore's executives say the card raised sales by encouraging their existing customers to buy more on each trip. That cannot be right, however, since the average amount Pellmore collected per transaction was essentially unchanged. The increase must therefore have come from the card's drawing new customers to Pellmore, most likely shoppers who had previously done their grocery shopping at Dunmore and who switched to take advantage of the discount.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, weakens the analyst's argument EXCEPT:
choices: Over the six months, customers who had already shopped at Pellmore the year before made substantially more trips to its stores than they had previously.
Dunmore's sales declines were concentrated in the product lines for which Pellmore's prices, after the card discount, were lower than Dunmore's.
In April, Dunmore closed a third of its stores in the region for renovations lasting the rest of the year.
Pellmore's sales in the six months before the card was introduced were also about 9 percent higher than in the same months a year earlier.
In March, Pellmore opened four new stores, and sales at those stores account for most of the chain's increase in total sales.
questions.explanation: The analyst concludes that the card drew new customers, probably from Dunmore. (B) does not weaken that: Dunmore losing sales exactly where the card made Pellmore cheaper is what the analyst's story predicts, so it strengthens. Each other choice offers a rival account: (A) more trips by existing customers (unchanged spending per transaction is consistent with that), (C) Dunmore closures pushing shoppers over regardless of the card, (D) growth that predates the card, and (E) new stores. (A) is the hardest to see, because the analyst ruled out only more spending per trip, not more trips.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The sales increase came from the card's drawing new customers to Pellmore, probably from Dunmore.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sales up 9 percent after the card; Dunmore down 4 percent; spending per transaction unchanged, so existing customers didn't buy more per trip.

breakdown.analysis: Four answers weaken; find the one that doesn't. The argument has two leaps: from 'not more per trip' to 'new customers' (it ignores more trips by old customers), and from 'new customers' to 'because of the card' (it ignores other reasons shoppers might come). Anything that fills either gap with a rival weakens. The odd one out will either be irrelevant or, as here, support the analyst.

choices.note: Weakens. Sales = transactions x spend per transaction. The analyst ruled out higher spend per trip but not more trips; if existing customers came more often, no new customers are needed.
CORRECT. This fits the analyst's story perfectly: shoppers left Dunmore precisely where the discounted card prices undercut it. It supports the conclusion rather than weakening it.
Weakens. Shoppers displaced by Dunmore's closures would come to Pellmore whether or not there was a card, so the new customers need not have been drawn by the card.
Weakens. If sales were already growing 9 percent a year before the card existed, the post-card growth needn't be due to the card at all.
Weakens. New stores bring in new sales without any help from the card, so the increase is explained by expansion rather than by the card's pull.

questions.stimulus: Arts administrator: The national endowment awards touring grants only to ensembles that document a matching commitment from the government of the city in which they are based. Our city will make no matching commitment to any arts organization except one that holds a signed partnership agreement with the city's school district, and the district signs such agreements only with organizations that give at least ten free performances in its schools each year. The Riverside Chamber Orchestra's musicians' contract, which cannot be reopened before it expires two years from now, permits the orchestra no more than six unpaid performances a year, and every performance given under the orchestra's name is covered by that contract. Several board members insist that the orchestra's acclaimed touring history makes its application a strong one, and perhaps it does. Nevertheless, however strong its proposal, the orchestra cannot receive a touring grant in the current funding cycle.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the arts administrator's argument depends?
choices: If the city made a matching commitment to the orchestra, the endowment would award the orchestra a touring grant.
The orchestra will not give any free performances in the city's schools during the current funding cycle.
The school district has never signed a partnership agreement with an organization whose performers' contract limited its unpaid performances.
A performance given in the district's schools free of charge would count as an unpaid performance under the musicians' contract.
The orchestra's proposal would fail to satisfy at least one of the endowment's other criteria for awarding a touring grant.
questions.explanation: The chain runs: grant → city match → district agreement → ten free school performances. The orchestra is blocked only if it can't give ten free performances, and the contract limits UNPAID performances. 'Free' to the schools isn't the same as 'unpaid' to the musicians: a sponsor could pay the players. So the argument needs free school performances to count as unpaid ones (D). Negate (D) and the orchestra could give ten paid-for free performances, breaking the chain. (B) is too strong: the argument needs fewer than ten, not zero.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The orchestra cannot receive a touring grant this cycle.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Grant → city match → school-district agreement → ≥10 free school performances/yr. The musicians' contract (binding, covers all performances) allows ≤6 unpaid performances/yr.

breakdown.analysis: Line up the chain and look for the word change: the district needs FREE performances; the contract caps UNPAID ones. The argument works only if a free school performance is an unpaid one. Negation test: if free school performances could be paid (by a sponsor, say), the cap wouldn't touch them, the orchestra could give ten, and the conclusion collapses. The contract-reopening and 'all performances' gaps are already closed in the stimulus.

choices.note: This reverses the first link. The argument needs 'grant → match', not 'match → grant'. Negated (a match wouldn't guarantee a grant), the argument is unaffected.
Too strong. The argument needs only that the orchestra can't reach ten. Negated (it will give a few free performances), it could still be capped at six.
History of the district's past agreements isn't required. Negated (the district once signed with such an organization), the current rule still demands ten free performances.

CORRECT. Negate it: free school performances wouldn't count against the six-performance cap. Then the orchestra could give ten (paid by someone other than the schools), earn the district agreement and the city match, and the conclusion fails.
The argument expressly sets the merits aside ('however strong its proposal'). Negated (the proposal meets every other criterion), the chain still blocks the grant.

questions.stimulus: Newspaper editor: Our reporter Dana Ortiz has obtained a draft of the city's budget from a staff member who was not authorized to release it. Leaked government documents are often worth publishing because they expose official misconduct, but this draft exposes none: it merely shows that the mayor is weighing cuts to the library system, cuts she has publicly declined to rule out. Ortiz argues that residents deserve to know about the proposed cuts before the council's budget vote on Tuesday, and she is right that the information could change how residents lobby their council members. But the city will release the draft officially on Monday morning, which leaves residents time to act before the vote, and publishing it today would almost certainly identify the staff member, who would then lose her job. We should therefore not publish the draft today.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the newspaper editor's reasoning?
choices: A newspaper should publish a leaked government document whenever its contents could affect how citizens act before an impending vote.

A newspaper should not publish a leaked government document that reveals no misconduct if doing so would cost its source a job, unless the document concerns a matter on which public officials are scheduled to vote within the next several days.

A newspaper should not publish a leaked government document that reveals no misconduct if doing so would cost its source a job, unless the public could not otherwise learn the document's contents in time to act on them.
A newspaper should not publish a leaked government document that reveals official misconduct if doing so would expose its source to dismissal.
A newspaper should not publish a leaked government document if doing so would expose its source to criminal prosecution, unless the document reveals official misconduct.
questions.explanation: The editor's case turns on three facts: the draft shows no misconduct, publishing would cost the source her job, and the public will get the draft Monday, in time to act. (C) forbids publication in exactly that case unless the public couldn't otherwise learn in time, and the Monday release means the exception doesn't apply. (B) has the same rule with a different exception, and the pending Tuesday vote triggers it, so (B) would permit publication.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the principle that, applied to the facts, yields 'don't publish today'.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: We should not publish the draft today.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: No misconduct revealed; publication would cost the source her job; official release Monday leaves time to act before Tuesday's vote. (Concession: the information could affect lobbying.)

breakdown.analysis: Map each principle's trigger and exception onto the facts. The trigger must fit (no misconduct, job loss) and the exception must FAIL to apply. The editor's distinctive move is the timing point (official release Monday, before the vote), so the right exception is one that the timing defeats. Watch for principles that use 'misconduct' or 'prosecution' where the facts say otherwise.

choices.note: This supports Ortiz, not the editor: the draft could affect how residents act before the vote, so this principle calls for publication.
Near miss. The trigger fits, but the exception is satisfied (the council votes Tuesday), so this principle permits publication.
CORRECT. Trigger met: no misconduct, and the source would lose her job. Exception not met: the Monday release lets the public learn the contents in time to act. So the newspaper should not publish.
Applies only to documents that DO reveal misconduct. This draft reveals none, so the principle is silent.
The source faces dismissal, not criminal prosecution, so the trigger isn't met and the principle says nothing about this case.

questions.stimulus: Archivist: A letter in the Holm collection, signed by the merchant Ilse Varga, refers to "the new bridge at Kestel." Kestel's first bridge was completed in 1612 and was called the new bridge only until a second bridge opened in 1640, after which it was known as the old bridge. Parish records show that Varga died in 1638. The letter, however, is written on paper bearing a watermark used by the Dorn paper mill, which was founded in 1644 and began using that watermark in 1645. Some scholars have concluded that the letter is a forgery. But a forger working after 1645 would have had to know that the bridge was once called the new bridge, a usage that appears in no published source and that had long since fallen out of speech. So the most reasonable conclusion is that ______
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the archivist's argument?
choices: the document in the Holm collection was written out by Varga herself sometime between 1612 and 1638.
the document in the Holm collection is a copy, made no earlier than 1645, of a letter Varga composed before her death.
the Dorn mill must have used its watermark on some paper before 1645.
the forger of the letter had access to unpublished records from Kestel.
the bridge completed in 1612 was still sometimes called the new bridge after 1640.
questions.explanation: The wording ('new bridge') points to composition before 1640, and Varga's death puts it before 1638; the watermark puts the physical document after 1645. The only way to honor both, while rejecting forgery as the archivist does, is that the surviving sheet is a later copy of a genuine letter, as (B) says. (A) is the near-miss: it gets the composition date right but has Varga herself writing out this very sheet, which the 1645 paper rules out. (C) and (E) contradict the stated facts, and (D) adopts the forgery view the archivist rejects.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: Bridge called 'new' only 1612-1640; Varga died 1638; the paper's watermark dates from 1645 or later; the 'new bridge' usage was unpublished and obsolete after 1640.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Blank: the most reasonable conclusion, given that the forgery hypothesis is rejected.

breakdown.analysis: Two dates pull in opposite directions: the words say before 1638, the paper says after 1645. The archivist has just argued against forgery, so the blank must reconcile genuine words with late paper.
