Separate the text from the physical sheet: a genuine text can survive on later paper if someone copied it. Watch for answers that settle one date by contradicting the other fact.

choices.note: Near-miss. The text was composed then, but this sheet can't have been written out by Varga at all: its paper didn't exist until 1645, seven years after her death. The choice ignores the watermark the archivist must account for.
CORRECT. A later copy explains the 1645 paper while preserving Varga's genuine wording, which the archivist has just argued no later forger could have produced.
Contradicts the facts: the mill didn't even exist before 1644, and the archivist states it began using the watermark in 1645.
This rescues the forgery hypothesis, the opposite of where the archivist is heading.
Contradicts the stated fact that the bridge was called the old bridge after 1640, and even if true, Varga died in 1638, so it wouldn't explain the 1645 paper.

questions.stimulus: School board member: Three years ago our district dropped the requirement that students obtain a teacher's recommendation before enrolling in advanced calculus; now any student who requests the course may take it. Nothing else about the course has changed: the syllabus, the final examination, and the four instructors are all the same as before. Yet the proportion of enrolled students who pass the final examination has fallen from 81 percent to 68 percent. Defenders of open enrollment reply that the number of students passing the examination each year has nearly doubled. That reply misses the point. The policy's supporters promised that opening the course would not dilute it, and a thirteen-point drop in the pass rate, under an unchanged examination and unchanged instructors, shows that the course now teaches its students less effectively than it did before the policy took effect.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the school board member's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: confuses a decline in the proportion of enrolled students who pass the examination with a decline in the number of students who pass it
fails to establish that the instructors have taught the course in the same way throughout the period, rather than merely that they are the same instructors
overlooks the possibility that the course teaches each kind of student it enrolls as well as it ever did even though its overall pass rate has fallen
treats the defenders' claim about the number of students who pass as false on the grounds that it is irrelevant to the point in dispute
takes for granted that students who enroll without a recommendation are less likely to pass the examination than students who would have been recommended
questions.explanation: Open enrollment changed who takes the course. If the newly admitted students pass at a lower rate, the overall pass rate falls even if every kind of student learns exactly as well as before, so the drop doesn't show the course teaches less effectively. (C) names that mix effect. (E) is the trap: the argument doesn't assume the new students do worse; it ignores that possibility, which is the very thing that sinks it. (A) describes a confusion the argument explicitly avoids.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The course now teaches its students less effectively than before the policy.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pass rate fell from 81% to 68%; syllabus, exam, and instructors unchanged; (rebuttal) the doubled number of passers is beside the point.

breakdown.analysis: The policy changed the mix of students: it added a group (students who wouldn't have been recommended) that may pass at a lower rate. A blended rate can fall while each group's rate holds steady or even rises. The board member rules out changes in the course itself but never considers the change in who takes it. Prephrase: the drop could be entirely a composition effect. Watch for an answer that turns this oversight into an assumption the argument 'takes for granted'; the argument assumes the opposite.

choices.note: The board member expressly separates the two figures ('That reply misses the point') and argues from the proportion. No confusion between them occurs.
If the instructors taught worse, that would help the conclusion, not hurt it. Failing to show that teaching stayed the same isn't a weakness in an argument that the course got worse.

CORRECT. The overall rate is a blend of rates for different kinds of students. Adding a lower-passing group pulls the blend down even if the course serves every group as well as before, so a falling pass rate doesn't show less effective teaching.
The argument calls the reply beside the point, not false. It even leaves the doubling unchallenged.
Near miss. The argument doesn't take this for granted; if it were true, it would explain the drop and undercut the conclusion. The flaw is ignoring this possibility, not assuming it.

questions.stimulus: Journal editor: A scientific journal should publish a submitted replication study whenever the study both tests a finding that the journal itself previously published and follows a protocol that was publicly registered before any of its data were collected, unless the study departs from the original study's methods in some respect for which its authors offer no adequate justification. Journals that publish striking findings take on a responsibility to publish serious attempts to check them, and that responsibility does not depend on whether the attempt succeeds, fails, or merely produces an unremarkable result. Registering the protocol before collecting data keeps replicators from tailoring their analyses to a desired outcome, while the exception keeps a careless or poorly designed study from discrediting sound work. Some colleagues worry that such a policy would fill journals with dull papers, but that is a price worth paying.
questions.stem: The principle stated above, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choices: The Review of Behavioral Economics should publish Dr. Amin's replication study. It tests a finding that was first published in a rival journal and was later discussed at length in an article in the Review's own pages, its protocol was registered before data collection, and it follows the original methods exactly.

Dr. Bale's replication study tests a finding this journal published and follows a protocol registered before data collection began. But it changed the original study's dosage without any explanation. So this journal should reject Dr. Bale's study.

Dr. Chen's replication of a finding this journal published follows the original methods exactly, and its protocol was registered shortly after the first few participants had been tested. Since its result is unremarkable but sound, the journal should publish it.

Dr. Diaz's study, which found no effect, attempts to replicate a finding this journal published. Its protocol was registered before any data were collected. The original used sums of money in a currency no longer in circulation, so, as the paper explains, Diaz converted them to current amounts of equal purchasing power. So the journal should publish it.

Dr. Evans's replication study tests a finding this journal published, follows the original methods exactly, and was registered before any data were collected. But because that finding has already been replicated twice elsewhere, this journal is under no obligation to publish it.
questions.explanation: Publication is required when (1) the study tests the journal's own finding, (2) its protocol was registered before any data were collected, and (3) there's no unjustified departure from the original methods. (D) meets all three: the one departure, converting an obsolete currency, comes with an explanation that is plainly adequate, and the null result doesn't matter. (C) is the near-miss: registering after the first participants were tested fails 'before any of its data were collected'.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Principle: publish IF the study tests the journal's own earlier finding AND its protocol was registered before ANY data were collected, UNLESS it departs from the original methods without adequate justification. The result (positive, negative, unremarkable) is irrelevant.

breakdown.analysis: Turn the principle into a checklist: (1) the journal's own finding? (2) registered before any data? (3) any departure, and if so, justified? The principle only says when to publish, so a choice concluding 'reject' can't be justified by it, and a choice that excuses the journal when all three are met contradicts it. Read the time words closely: 'before any' is strict.

choices.note: Fails the first condition. The finding first appeared in a rival journal; discussing it later doesn't make it one this journal published.
The exception applies, so the principle doesn't require publication. But it says nothing about rejecting, so it can't justify 'should reject'.
The near-miss. The protocol was registered after the first participants were tested, so not 'before any of its data were collected'. The second condition fails.

CORRECT. Its own finding: yes. Registered before any data: yes. The one departure (converting an obsolete currency to equal purchasing power) is explained and keeps the original incentives intact, so the exception doesn't apply. A null result is no bar. The principle requires publication.
All three elements are met, so the principle requires publication. Earlier replications elsewhere don't matter, and the editor rejects a novelty requirement. This contradicts the principle.

questions.stimulus: Critic: Admittedly, the restored frescoes in the Varnell Chapel are brighter than any living visitor has seen them, and the restorers removed nothing but grime and later overpainting. Even so, the chapel's trustees were wrong to approve the restoration in the form it finally took. The trustees' own charter obliges them to preserve the chapel as its builders intended it to be experienced. The builders lit the chapel only with candles, and the painters designed the frescoes to be seen dimly, in flickering light, even exaggerating the contrasts in the figures' faces so that they would read clearly in the gloom. Under the bright electric lighting the restorers installed, those exaggerations look harsh and crude. It follows that the restored chapel no longer presents the frescoes as the builders meant them to be seen. Some defend the project by pointing out that visitors prefer the brighter view, but the charter does not make visitors' preferences the standard.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion drawn in the critic's argument?
choices: The restored chapel no longer presents the frescoes as the chapel's builders intended them to be seen.
The chapel's trustees were wrong to approve any restoration at all of the frescoes in the Varnell Chapel.
The trustees should not have approved the restoration as it was ultimately carried out.
The restorers removed nothing from the frescoes except grime and later overpainting.
Visitors' preference for a brighter view of the frescoes is not the standard set by the trustees' charter.
questions.explanation: The second sentence states the main conclusion: the trustees were wrong to approve the restoration in the form it took. Everything after it supports that claim, including the intermediate conclusion that the chapel no longer presents the frescoes as intended, which combines with the charter to yield the verdict. (B) is the near-miss: 'any restoration' overstates a conclusion aimed at the form the restoration took (the lighting in particular). (A) is the intermediate conclusion, (D) is the concession, and (E) is a rebuttal to an objection.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The trustees were wrong to approve the restoration in the form it finally took.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The charter requires preserving the chapel as its builders intended; the frescoes were made for candlelight; the new electric lighting makes them look crude; so the chapel no longer presents them as intended (intermediate conclusion). Concession: the cleaning removed only grime and overpainting. Rebuttal: visitor preference isn't the charter's standard.

breakdown.analysis: The 'It follows that' sentence near the end looks like the conclusion, but ask what it's for: it supports the claim that the trustees were wrong, via the charter. The verdict sits in sentence two, right after 'Even so', which pivots away from the concession. Then check scope: the critic concedes the cleaning was fine and objects to the restoration as completed, so the correct answer can't condemn every restoration.

choices.note: The intermediate conclusion. It's supported by the lighting premises and in turn supports the verdict on the trustees, so it isn't the main point.
Near-miss on one word. The critic concedes the cleaning was faithful and objects to the restoration 'in the form it finally took'; 'any restoration' claims far more.
CORRECT. A paraphrase of the sentence after 'Even so': approving the restoration as it was carried out was wrong. The rest of the argument supports this.
The concession, introduced by 'Admittedly', which the critic grants and then argues past.
A premise used to rebut an objection at the end; it defends the main conclusion rather than being it.

passages.title: Hadley, The Achilleas, and assumed responsibility
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Since Hadley v. Baxendale (1854), the common law has limited the damages recoverable for breach of contract to losses that arise naturally from the breach or that both parties could reasonably have contemplated, when they made the contract, as a probable result of it. The limitation was justified as a protection for promisors against risks they had no opportunity to price or guard against: the carrier in Hadley, never told that the mill's operation depended on the prompt return of its only crankshaft, was not liable for the profits lost while the mill stood idle. Later English decisions recast the test as a question of degree. A loss was recoverable if, given what the defendant knew at the time of contracting, it was "not unlikely" to result from breach, a standard the House of Lords in The Heron II (1969) made deliberately more demanding than the reasonable foreseeability that suffices in tort, on the ground that contracting parties, unlike strangers, can protect themselves by disclosing unusual risks before they bargain.

This probabilistic framing was challenged in Transfield Shipping v. Mercator Shipping (2008), known as The Achilleas. A charterer returned a vessel nine days late, by which time freight rates had collapsed; the owner, forced to reduce the rate on its next charter in order to keep that engagement, claimed the reduction over the whole of the later charter rather than only the difference between market and contract rates for the nine days of delay. The arbitrators found the larger loss to be of a kind that was not unlikely to result, yet the House of Lords unanimously limited recovery, though its members did not all give the same reasons. Lord Hoffmann's reasoning was the most ambitious. Because the limits of contractual liability were, in his view, a matter of interpreting the agreement as a whole, the question was what liability a reasonable person in the promisor's position would have understood himself to be undertaking, and the evidence indicated a general understanding in the shipping market that a charterer who redelivered late answered only for the overrun period. Foreseeability, on this view, is merely evidence of an assumed responsibility, which it usually, but not invariably, tracks.

Hoffmann's diagnosis seems to me largely correct. The Heron II's own rationale, that parties can bargain over the risks they foresee, presupposes that the rule exists to allocate risk in accordance with the bargain, and probability is therefore only a means to that end. Nor is it evident why a party should bear a loss merely because the loss was likely, if the trade in which the contract was made has settled on a different allocation. Yet to adopt assumption of responsibility as the general test would invite the very uncertainty that the Hadley formula was devised to curb. Whether a party "assumed" a risk is a question on which litigants can always offer competing reconstructions of what reasonable merchants would have intended, and American courts, having experimented with a comparable "tacit agreement" test associated with Justice Holmes, largely abandoned it; the drafters of the Uniform Commercial Code expressly rejected it.

The better course, and the one that subsequent English decisions have generally taken, is to treat Hoffmann's inquiry not as a replacement for the probability test but as a qualification of it. A loss that was not unlikely remains presumptively recoverable unless there is evidence, of the kind found in The Achilleas, of a recognized understanding in the relevant market that excludes it. So confined, the inquiry into assumed responsibility can correct the probability test where it miscarries without requiring courts, in every dispute, to reconstruct what the parties would have agreed to about a question they never considered.

passages.title: The Hubble tension
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
The present rate of cosmic expansion, the Hubble constant, can be estimated by two largely independent routes, and for roughly a decade the routes have disagreed. The first infers the constant from the cosmic microwave background: the Planck satellite's measurements of the angular scale of acoustic oscillations imprinted when the universe was some 380,000 years old, interpreted through the standard cosmological model, yield a value near 67 kilometers per second per megaparsec. The second, the "distance ladder," works outward from the nearby universe: geometric parallaxes calibrate the luminosities of Cepheid variable stars, Cepheids in galaxies that have hosted Type Ia supernovae calibrate the luminosities of those supernovae, and supernovae far enough away to be carried by the smooth cosmic expansion then yield the rate directly. The ladder assembled by the SH0ES collaboration gives a value near 73, and the stated uncertainties of the two results are now small enough that chance is no longer a credible explanation of the gap.

Two kinds of explanation have been advanced. On the first, the discrepancy signals physics absent from the standard model, most prominently a transient "early dark energy" that would have briefly hastened expansion before the microwave background was released, shrinking the sound horizon that serves as that background's standard ruler and thereby raising the constant inferred from it. On the second, the ladder harbors an undiagnosed systematic error. Suspicion fell chiefly on the Cepheids, which in distant galaxies are observed against crowded stellar fields whose unresolved light could make them appear brighter, and hence nearer, than they are. The Carnegie-Chicago Hubble Program, recalibrating the supernovae with an independent standard (the luminosity at which red giant stars ignite helium in their cores, known as the tip of the red giant branch), obtained an intermediate value near 70, and some took this as evidence that the Cepheid rung was at fault.

Neither explanation has fared as well as its proponents hoped. Early dark energy can raise the inferred constant, but the versions that do so tend to worsen agreement with measurements of how matter has clustered, and they must be tuned to switch on and off at precisely the epoch at which they would do the most good, a feature that makes them less a prediction than an accommodation. The systematic-error hypothesis has suffered more directly: observations with the James Webb Space Telescope, whose sharper infrared images largely resolve the crowding around distant Cepheids, have closely reproduced the earlier Cepheid measurements, removing the most specific mechanism by which the ladder was supposed to have erred.

It would be premature, however, to conclude that the discrepancy must therefore reflect new physics. That the Cepheid measurements survive scrutiny does not show that the ladder as a whole is sound: the persistent disagreement between Cepheid-based and red-giant-based calibrations, which largely share their supernovae and differ chiefly in their stellar rungs, indicates that the ladder's error budget does not yet capture all of its systematic uncertainty, even if it does not reveal where the error lies. What the debate most needs is not a further refinement of either rung but a determination of the constant that shares none of the ladder's assumptions. Gravitational-wave "standard sirens," whose distances follow from general relativity rather than from any stellar calibration, promise such a determination, though the few events observed so far constrain the constant too loosely to adjudicate between the competing values. Until such measurements mature, the most defensible position is that the discrepancy is real as a disagreement between methods but undetermined as to its cause.

passages.title: Las Meninas and its mirror
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Velázquez's Las Meninas (1656) shows the young Infanta Margarita among her attendants in a high room of the Madrid palace. To the left the painter himself stands behind an enormous canvas whose face is turned away from us; at the back, beside a lit doorway in which a court official pauses on the stairs, a small mirror holds the dim half-length figures of King Philip IV and Queen Mariana. Because the painter and several of his subjects gaze outward, toward the place the beholder occupies, and because the mirror appears to return the image of whoever stands there, the picture has long been read as a reflection on its own viewing. Three accounts of that reflexivity have shaped modern discussion.

For Michel Foucault, whose analysis opens The Order of Things (1966), the painting represents classical representation itself. Everything that belongs to the act of depiction is laid out before us—the painter, his instruments, the gazes of the models—except the figure toward whom all of it converges: the sovereign who is at once the model being painted, the spectator of the scene, and the point from which it is seen. He appears only as a faint reflection, and the place he occupies is, in Foucault's phrase, an essential void. John Searle (1980) turned the same configuration into a logical puzzle. Illusionistic pictures, he argued, obey the rule that a picture shows its scene from the point at which the painter stood; Las Meninas seems to be painted from the place of the royal couple, yet it shows its painter elsewhere, working, so that it appears both to be and not to be the picture he is painting. The work, Searle concluded, violates the very conventions on which it depends.

Joel Snyder and Ted Cohen replied that the puzzle rests on a mistake of fact. Reconstructing the room's perspective, they placed the vanishing point not in the mirror but in the doorway, near the arm of the official standing there, and argued that, given that geometry, the mirror cannot be reflecting figures who stand where the beholder stands. What it reflects, they proposed, is the front of the great canvas on which the painter is at work, a canvas that therefore depicts the king and queen. Once the reflection is understood as an image of a painted image, nothing obliges us to suppose that the picture is painted from the couple's place, and Searle's paradox dissolves. Las Meninas, on their account, is an extraordinary picture but not an impossible one.

On the geometry I believe Snyder and Cohen are right, and their correction disposes of Searle's paradox more completely than his defenders have conceded: a contradiction that depends on a misplaced vanishing point is a contradiction in the beholder's report, not in the picture. It does not follow, however, that the reflexivity critics have found in the work is merely an illusion that measurement dispels, as Snyder and Cohen seem to conclude. What their analysis establishes is that the painting reliably induces an error—almost every viewer takes the mirror to show the royal couple standing where the viewer stands—and that only a reconstruction no one performs while looking can correct it. Such a misreading is too predictable to be an accident of reception. Velázquez set the reflection exactly where the eye would most readily mistake it for a reflection of the beholder's own position, and the experience Foucault describes depends on that mistake.

Foucault, accordingly, described the experience of the picture more faithfully than he explained it. The void he found is not a feature of the depicted space, which is wholly coherent, but of the encounter between that space and the viewer it is built to mislead. A satisfactory account of Las Meninas must therefore join the geometry that Snyder and Cohen supplied to an account of looking that geometry by itself cannot provide.

passages.title: The democratic peace and its sources
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Passage A

Few findings in the study of international politics have proved as durable as the observation that established democracies have almost never fought wars against one another. Michael Doyle, who drew attention to the pattern in the early 1980s, traced the underlying idea to Kant's sketch of a federation of republics in Perpetual Peace, and since Doyle's work Bruce Russett and others subjected it to systematic test, the regularity has survived repeated disputes over how democracy and war should be defined: the few apparent exceptions involve states whose democratic credentials were doubtful or hostilities too limited to count as war by the conventional threshold of battle deaths. Notably, democracies are not in general less warlike than other states; they fight nondemocracies about as often as other states do. The peace is a property of the pair, not of the regime.

One must ask whether something other than regime type produces the pattern. Wealth, alliance ties, and geographic distance are all correlated with democracy, and each may independently reduce the risk of conflict between two states. Yet in studies that control for these factors, the estimated effect of joint democracy shrinks without disappearing. Some of the raw association, in other words, belongs to democracy's companions; a substantial remainder does not, and it is the remainder that requires explanation. Two mechanisms have been proposed to explain it: leaders answerable to voters who bear the costs of war face institutional obstacles to fighting, and democracies extend to one another the norms of negotiated compromise they practice at home. Their relative weight remains unsettled, and neither accounts for every case. But an association that persists under such controls warrants the expectation that a world containing more democracies will see fewer wars among them.

Passage B

That pairs of democracies have rarely fought one another is not in dispute; what the fact shows is. In an influential 1995 study, Henry Farber and Joanne Gowa found that the pacific effect of joint democracy is confined largely to the years after 1945. Before the First World War, democratic pairs were not significantly less likely than other pairs to become embroiled in militarized disputes, even if few of those disputes escalated to war. After 1945 the effect is strong—but this was a period in which most democracies shared an overriding interest in opposing the Soviet Union, and states united against a common adversary have compelling reasons not to fight one another whatever their constitutions. Controlling for formal alliances does not resolve the difficulty, because common interests extend well beyond treaty commitments. Alliances are only the most visible expression of a shared stake in a particular international order, and states may hold such a stake, and act on it, without having signed anything that a researcher could code.

None of this shows that democracy is irrelevant to peace, and Farber and Gowa did not claim that it does; their argument concerns what the post-1945 evidence can be made to prove. Accountability to electorates and habits of domestic compromise may well make democratic leaders slower to fight than autocrats. The question is whether those dispositions would suffice to keep democracies at peace with one another once the interests that bound them together diverged. The record of a single era in which institutions and interests coincided cannot settle it, and policies that promote democracy abroad in the expectation of peace rest on an answer the evidence does not yet supply.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The probability-based test of remoteness should give way to an inquiry into the liability that a contracting party reasonably understood itself to be undertaking.
The Achilleas departed from Hadley v. Baxendale by holding that a loss that was not unlikely to result from breach may be unrecoverable when it arises in a volatile market.
Hoffmann rightly identifies what the remoteness rule is for, but his inquiry should override the probability test only where a settled market understanding requires it.
Neither the probability test nor the inquiry into assumed responsibility is justified by the purpose of the remoteness rule, which is better served by requiring the disclosure of unusual risks.
Because an inquiry into assumed responsibility would make outcomes uncertain, courts should continue to apply the probability test of The Heron II without modification.
questions.explanation: The author accepts Hoffmann's diagnosis ('largely correct', paragraph 3) but rejects it as a general test and endorses using it only as a qualification: a not-unlikely loss is 'presumptively recoverable unless there is evidence... of a recognized understanding in the relevant market that excludes it' (paragraph 4). C states both halves. A is Hoffmann's position, which the author refuses to generalize; E keeps only the author's reservation and drops the endorsement of the qualification.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the author's overall position, which combines partial agreement with Hoffmann and a limit on his test.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first and fourth sentences; paragraph 4, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Three positions: the traditional probability test (paragraph 1), Hoffmann's assumption-of-responsibility test (paragraph 2), and the author's view (paragraphs 3-4). The author says Hoffmann is right about what the rule is for, wrong to make his test general, and endorses a hybrid: probability test as the default, overridden by a recognized market understanding. A main point must carry both the agreement and the limit. Watch for answers that give only one of the two halves.

choices.note: Hoffmann's view, not the author's. The author says adopting assumption of responsibility 'as the general test' would invite uncertainty, and keeps the probability test as the default. Wrong position-holder.
A distorted detail. The passage never says the Lords rested on market volatility, and in any case this describes one case rather than the author's thesis.

CORRECT. 'Rightly identifies what the remoteness rule is for' = 'Hoffmann's diagnosis seems to me largely correct'; 'only where a settled market understanding requires it' = 'presumptively recoverable unless... a recognized understanding in the relevant market that excludes it.'
Contradicts paragraph 3: the author says The Heron II's rationale supports Hoffmann's account of the rule's purpose, and the author endorses a qualified test rather than a disclosure requirement.
Half right. The author does worry about uncertainty, but explicitly endorses qualifying the probability test, so 'without modification' is the opposite of the author's conclusion.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about the dispute in The Achilleas, considered under the approach the author recommends in the final paragraph?
choices: The owner would have recovered the reduction over the whole later charter, since the arbitrators found that loss not unlikely to result.
The outcome would have turned on whether the owner had told the charterer, when they contracted, about the owner's next charter.
The charterer would have been liable only for the overrun period, but only because the larger loss was not in fact likely to result.
The owner would have had to show that the charterer had tacitly agreed to bear the loss on the later charter.
The owner's recovery would still have been limited, because of evidence of a market understanding excluding the larger loss.
questions.explanation: Under the author's approach a not-unlikely loss is presumptively recoverable 'unless there is evidence, of the kind found in The Achilleas, of a recognized understanding in the relevant market that excludes it' (paragraph 4, second sentence). Paragraph 2 says that evidence existed, so the presumption is rebutted and recovery stays limited: E. A applies only the presumption and ignores the exception.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's recommended rule to the facts of The Achilleas.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, third and fifth sentences; paragraph 4, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Two steps. (1) Under the author's rule, start with the probability test: the arbitrators found the larger loss 'not unlikely', so it is presumptively recoverable. (2) Then ask whether there is evidence of a market understanding that excludes it. Paragraph 2 says 'the evidence indicated a general understanding in the shipping market' that a late charterer answered only for the overrun, and paragraph 4 explicitly points to The Achilleas as having evidence 'of the kind' that rebuts the presumption. So same result as the Lords, for the author's reason.

choices.note: The trap. It runs step one and stops. The author's rule has an exception, and paragraph 4 names The Achilleas as the model case for that exception.
Disclosure matters to the baseline probability test, but nothing makes the outcome 'turn on' it here: even a not-unlikely loss is excluded by the market understanding.
Right result, wrong reason. The arbitrators found the loss not unlikely, and nothing in the passage disputes that finding; under the author's rule the limit comes from the market understanding.
That is the Holmes 'tacit agreement' test, which the passage says American courts abandoned and which the author cites as a warning, not a model.
CORRECT. Paragraph 4: presumptively recoverable 'unless there is evidence, of the kind found in The Achilleas, of a recognized understanding in the relevant market that excludes it.'

questions.stem: The author mentions the "tacit agreement" test (third paragraph, last sentence) primarily in order to
choices: back a reservation about Hoffmann's test as a general rule by citing a comparable test's fate
suggest that Lord Hoffmann's reasoning in The Achilleas was borrowed from an American precedent
illustrate the kind of uncertainty that the Hadley formula was originally devised to curb
show that American and English courts have converged on a probability-based test of remoteness
concede that an inquiry of the kind Hoffmann proposed has been adopted in at least one other jurisdiction
questions.explanation: The sentence follows the author's 'Yet' (paragraph 3, fourth sentence): making assumed responsibility the general test 'would invite the very uncertainty' Hadley was meant to curb. The reference to a 'comparable' test that American courts abandoned and the UCC rejected backs that reservation, which is A. C is the near miss: the Holmes test came after Hadley, and the passage presents it as the outcome to avoid, not as what Hadley was devised against.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what job the tacit-agreement reference does in the author's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, fourth and fifth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before it: the paragraph pivots on 'Yet', from agreeing with Hoffmann to resisting his test as a general standard. The last sentence then gives two reasons: litigants can always offer competing reconstructions, and a 'comparable' test was abandoned in America and rejected by the UCC drafters. So the reference is evidence for the reservation. Prephrase: 'precedent showing that this kind of test did not last.'

choices.note: CORRECT. The 'tacit agreement' test is called 'comparable' to Hoffmann's, and its abandonment and rejection back the author's reservation about adopting assumed responsibility 'as the general test.'
'Comparable' is not 'borrowed from'. The passage says nothing about where Hoffmann's reasoning came from.

Near miss. It borrows the phrase from the preceding sentence, but Hadley (1854) could not have been devised against a later test, and the passage never says the tacit-agreement test produced uncertainty. The reference supports a prediction about Hoffmann's test; it doesn't illustrate Hadley's purpose.
Unsupported. The passage says only that American courts abandoned one test; it doesn't say what they adopted or compare them with English courts.
The reverse. The reference shows a similar inquiry being abandoned, not adopted.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Lord Hoffmann's reasoning in The Achilleas can most accurately be described as
choices: unqualified endorsement of both its account of the remoteness rule's purpose and the test it proposes
doubt about its account of the remoteness rule's purpose, combined with approval of the result it reached
grudging acceptance of it as the least objectionable of several flawed approaches to remoteness
agreement with its account of what the rule is for, tempered by doubt about making it the general test
respect for its ambition, coupled with the conviction that it misread the rationale of The Heron II
questions.explanation: The author calls Hoffmann's 'diagnosis' 'largely correct' and argues that The Heron II's own rationale shows the rule exists to allocate risk according to the bargain (paragraph 3). But the author objects that 'to adopt assumption of responsibility as the general test would invite the very uncertainty' Hadley was meant to curb. D captures both. B reverses which part is accepted; E reverses how The Heron II's rationale relates to Hoffmann.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pin down the author's mixed attitude to Hoffmann: which part is accepted and which part is resisted.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 in full; paragraph 4, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Split Hoffmann into (1) a diagnosis: remoteness is about assumed responsibility, and foreseeability is only evidence of it; (2) a remedy: use assumed responsibility as the test. The author accepts (1) ('largely correct') and resists (2) as a general rule, keeping it only as a 'qualification'. The right answer has to say agree on (1), limit (2).

choices.note: Too strong. 'Yet to adopt assumption of responsibility as the general test would invite the very uncertainty...' is a clear qualification.

Reversed. The author accepts the account of the rule's purpose; what the author doubts is the test, not the purpose. And the passage gives the author's reasons for the result rather than simply approving it.
Wrong tone and wrong content. The author doesn't reluctantly settle for Hoffmann's approach; the author endorses something different, the probability test qualified by Hoffmann's inquiry.
CORRECT. 'Account of what the rule is for' = Hoffmann's 'diagnosis', which is 'largely correct'; 'doubt about making it the general test' = the objection to adopting it 'as the general test.'

'Most ambitious' is in the passage, but the author argues that The Heron II's rationale supports Hoffmann ('presupposes that the rule exists to allocate risk in accordance with the bargain'), not that Hoffmann misread it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the approach to remoteness that the author recommends in the final paragraph?
choices: A sports league abolishes its rulebook penalties and directs officials to decide each case by asking what the players would have agreed to had they considered the matter.
A league penalizes a foul as its rulebook prescribes, unless officials find a long-recognized convention among players that treats such contact as ordinary play.
A league applies its rulebook penalties strictly and refuses to hear evidence of any convention among its players about what contact is acceptable.
A league penalizes a foul only if the player who committed it had expressly agreed in advance to accept the penalty for that kind of contact.
A league allows any penalty to be waived if both the player who committed the foul and the player who suffered it consent after the game.
questions.explanation: The author's approach has a default (a not-unlikely loss is 'presumptively recoverable') that is displaced only by 'evidence... of a recognized understanding in the relevant market that excludes it.' B has the same shape: the rulebook default applies unless a recognized convention in the relevant community excludes it. A is the analogue of Hoffmann's test made general, which the author rejects; C is the unqualified probability test.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the case with the same structure as the author's recommended rule.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first and second sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the rule: (1) a general default criterion governs; (2) it is displaced only by proof of a recognized understanding within the relevant community; (3) courts are not asked, in every case, to reconstruct what the parties would have agreed. Then match. Distinguish it from the other positions in the passage, each of which has an analogue among the wrong answers: Hoffmann-as-general-test (A), the probability test alone (C), the Holmes tacit-agreement test (D).

choices.note: The analogue of making assumed responsibility the general test, reconstructing in every case what the parties would have agreed. The author rejects exactly this.
CORRECT. Default rule (rulebook / probability test) applies unless there is a recognized understanding in the relevant community (players' convention / market understanding) that excludes it.
The probability test with no qualification: it shuts out the very evidence the author's approach makes decisive.
Mirrors the actual-agreement idea behind the Holmes test, which the passage treats as abandoned and the author does not endorse.
Consensual waiver after the fact has no counterpart in the passage; remoteness is fixed by what was understood at the time of contracting.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: A promisor who knew the facts that made a loss not unlikely to result from breach should be liable for that loss in every case.
The standard of foreseeability that applies in tort would serve parties who contract in volatile markets better than the Hadley test does.
The Heron II was mistaken to make the contractual standard of remoteness more demanding than the standard that applies in tort.
Disclosing unusual risks before contracting is the only means by which a promisor can limit its liability for losses that result from breach.
The reason The Heron II gave for its standard fits Hoffmann's account of the remoteness rule better than that standard itself does.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3, second sentence: The Heron II's rationale 'presupposes that the rule exists to allocate risk in accordance with the bargain, and probability is therefore only a means to that end.' So the case's rationale points toward Hoffmann's account, while its probability standard is the thing Hoffmann challenged. That is E. A is too strong: the author's rule excludes not-unlikely losses when a market understanding excludes them.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's own claims support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence; paragraph 3, second and third sentences; paragraph 4, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The author's distinctive move is turning The Heron II against itself: its reason for the stricter standard (parties can bargain over foreseen risks) shows that the rule is about allocating risk by the bargain, which is Hoffmann's point, so probability is 'only a means.' Look for an answer that captures that tension between the case's reason and the case's standard. Check absolute words ('every case', 'only').

choices.note: Too strong. In the author's rule a not-unlikely loss is only 'presumptively' recoverable, and it is excluded where a recognized market understanding excludes it, as in The Achilleas.
Nothing supports preferring the tort standard; the author never questions The Heron II's choice to make the contractual standard stricter.
The author doesn't criticize this feature of The Heron II and in fact builds on its rationale.
Extreme and unsupported. Disclosure is mentioned as one way parties can protect themselves, and the passage itself says a market understanding can limit liability without any disclosure.
CORRECT. The rationale 'presupposes that the rule exists to allocate risk in accordance with the bargain', which is Hoffmann's view, while the probability standard is 'only a means to that end.'

questions.stem: In saying that the inquiry into assumed responsibility can correct the probability test "where it miscarries" (last sentence of the passage), the author most probably refers to cases in which the probability test would
choices: impose liability for a not-unlikely loss that falls outside the allocation of risk recognized in the relevant trade
deny recovery for a loss that was likely to result from breach merely because the promisee had not disclosed it to the promisor
be applied by arbitrators instead of by a court that could consider evidence of market practice
reach a result different from the one that the standard applied in tort would reach on the same facts
deny recovery for a loss that both parties had in fact contemplated when they made their contract
questions.explanation: The only correction the final paragraph describes runs one way: a not-unlikely loss is presumptively recoverable 'unless there is evidence... of a recognized understanding in the relevant market that excludes it.' So the probability test 'miscarries' when it would impose liability that the trade's understood allocation excludes, as in The Achilleas: A. B and E describe the test wrongly denying recovery, the opposite direction.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what 'miscarries' refers to from the rule the sentence summarizes.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second and third sentences; paragraph 3, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: 'So confined' points back to the previous sentence, which says what Hoffmann's inquiry does: it excludes a not-unlikely loss when a recognized market understanding excludes it. Paragraph 3 makes the same point: it isn't evident why a party should bear a loss 'merely because the loss was likely, if the trade... has settled on a different allocation.' So the miscarriage is over-inclusion. Check the direction in every answer.

choices.note: CORRECT. Matches the exception in paragraph 4 and paragraph 3's objection to making a party 'bear a loss merely because the loss was likely' when the trade has 'settled on a different allocation.'
Wrong direction. The correction the author describes only removes liability that the probability test would impose; it never adds recovery.
Who applies the test is not the issue. The arbitrators and the Lords differed on the result, but 'miscarries' is about what the test yields, not who applies it.
The passage treats the stricter contractual standard as deliberate. Differing from tort is designed in, not a miscarriage.
Wrong direction again. And a loss the parties actually contemplated would satisfy the Hadley test, so the probability test would not deny it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Recent observations have confirmed the distance ladder's value for the Hubble constant, so the discrepancy must reflect physics absent from the standard cosmological model.
Calibrations based on red giant stars have resolved the discrepancy between the two estimates of the Hubble constant by yielding a value that lies between them.
Because proposals invoking early dark energy accommodate the data rather than predict them, the discrepancy is best attributed to systematic error in the distance ladder.
Although the leading explanations of the disagreement have each been weakened, it remains unsettled whether it stems from new physics or from measurement error.
The disagreement over the Hubble constant cannot be explained until gravitational-wave measurements replace the distance ladder as the principal means of determining it.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says 'Neither explanation has fared as well as its proponents hoped', and paragraph 4 concludes that the discrepancy is 'real as a disagreement between methods but undetermined as to its cause.' D says both. A is the conclusion the author calls 'premature'; C picks a side the author declines to pick; E turns 'what the debate most needs' into a strict requirement and adds 'replace'.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the author's overall conclusion about the Hubble tension.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first sentence; paragraph 4, first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Structure: the discrepancy (paragraph 1), two explanations (paragraph 2), both weakened (paragraph 3), the author's hedged verdict (paragraph 4): don't infer new physics, because the ladder may still have unrecognized systematics, and wait for independent measurements. The main point keeps the hedge: real discrepancy, cause unsettled. Reject any answer that picks a winner.

choices.note: The inference the author calls 'premature'. Also, JWST confirmed the Cepheid measurements, not the ladder as a whole: 'does not show that the ladder as a whole is sound.'
The red-giant value is described as intermediate, and its disagreement with the Cepheid calibration is 'persistent'. Nothing is resolved.
The first half is the author's criticism, but the conclusion overreaches. The author says the systematic-error hypothesis 'has suffered more directly' and refuses to assign a cause.
CORRECT. 'Each been weakened' = 'Neither explanation has fared as well as its proponents hoped'; 'remains unsettled' = 'undetermined as to its cause.'
Too strong. The author says sirens 'promise' a decisive independent determination; nothing says they must 'replace' the ladder or that nothing else could explain the discrepancy.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following?
choices: The value of the Hubble constant inferred from the microwave background does not depend on any assumption about the physics of the early universe.
If early dark energy did operate, the value inferred from the microwave background using the standard model would be too low.
The Cepheids in distant galaxies appear brighter than they are because of light from unresolved neighboring stars.
Calibrating supernovae with red giant stars is less susceptible to systematic error than calibrating them with Cepheids.
The uncertainties stated for the two estimates of the Hubble constant have been understated by roughly equal amounts.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2, second sentence: early dark energy would shrink the sound horizon, 'thereby raising the constant inferred from it.' So if it really operated, an inference that leaves it out (the standard model) would come out lower than the true value: B. D is the attractive assumption a reader brings to the red-giant result, but the passage never ranks the two methods' reliability, and paragraph 4 treats their disagreement as unexplained.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim that follows from the passage's statements.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, second sentence; paragraph 2, second, fourth and fifth sentences; paragraph 3, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Inference questions reward chasing a mechanism. The microwave background value is inferred 'through the standard cosmological model' using the sound horizon as a ruler. Early dark energy would shrink that ruler and raise the inferred constant. So the standard-model value would be an underestimate if early dark energy were real. Check each other answer against what the passage says, especially paragraph 3's JWST result.

choices.note: Contradicted. The value is obtained 'interpreted through the standard cosmological model', and paragraph 2 shows how a change in early-universe physics would change it.
CORRECT. Early dark energy would shrink the sound horizon, 'thereby raising the constant inferred from it'; an inference that omits it would therefore come out too low.
The crowding worry is stated only as a possibility ('could make them appear brighter'), and the JWST images, which 'largely resolve the crowding', reproduced the earlier measurements.
The trap. Some took the red-giant result as evidence against the Cepheids, but the author doesn't endorse that, and paragraph 4 says the disagreement 'does not reveal where the error lies.'
Nothing in the passage compares the size of any understatement. The author suggests only that the ladder's error budget may be incomplete.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: argue that the discrepancy described in the first paragraph arises from an error in the Cepheid rung of the distance ladder
describe the observations that first led researchers to propose the two explanations discussed in the second paragraph
evaluate the two explanations presented in the second paragraph and indicate that neither has been vindicated
defend the hypothesis of early dark energy against the objection that it must be finely tuned to fit the data
show that observations with the James Webb Space Telescope have established the reliability of the distance ladder as a whole
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens 'Neither explanation has fared as well as its proponents hoped' and then gives a problem for each: early dark energy worsens the fit to clustering and has to be tuned, and JWST removed the crowding mechanism for systematic error. C. E overstates the JWST result; paragraph 4 says the Cepheid result 'does not show that the ladder as a whole is sound.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe what paragraph 3 does in the passage's structure.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, all three sentences; paragraph 4, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 2 sets out two explanations. Paragraph 3 takes them in order and weakens each: its first sentence is a topic sentence that says so. Paragraph 4 then explains why the second explanation's setback doesn't hand victory to the first. The paragraph's job: assess both, crown neither.

choices.note: The opposite of what paragraph 3 reports: the JWST observations removed the most specific mechanism for a Cepheid error.
Paragraph 3 comes after the explanations were proposed and reports problems with them, not their origins.
CORRECT. The first sentence states the verdict ('Neither explanation has fared as well...'), and the next two sentences support it for each explanation in turn.
The paragraph raises the tuning point as an objection ('less a prediction than an accommodation'); it doesn't defend against it.
Too strong, and the author denies it in the next paragraph: the Cepheid measurements surviving scrutiny 'does not show that the ladder as a whole is sound.'

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the claim that the disagreement over the Hubble constant reflects physics absent from the standard cosmological model can most accurately be described as
choices: firm rejection, on the ground that the modifications so far proposed conflict with other cosmological measurements
cautious endorsement, since the most specific alternative explanation of the disagreement has been undermined
indifference, since the author regards the cause of the disagreement as a question that observation cannot settle
confidence that the claim will be confirmed once gravitational-wave measurements become more precise
reserved judgment, combined with skepticism about the most prominent version of the claim proposed so far
questions.explanation: The author calls it 'premature' to conclude that the discrepancy reflects new physics and says its cause is 'undetermined' (paragraph 4), which is reserved judgment. The author also says early dark energy, the 'most prominent' proposal (paragraph 2), is 'less a prediction than an accommodation' (paragraph 3), which is skepticism. E. B is the trap: it repeats the reasoning the author warns against in paragraph 4.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the author's stance on the new-physics explanation, precisely.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, second sentence; paragraph 3, second sentence; paragraph 4, first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Two signals. First, the author criticizes early dark energy, the 'most prominent' new-physics proposal, as tuned and as worsening other fits. Second, the author refuses to conclude either way: 'premature... to conclude that the discrepancy must therefore reflect new physics', 'undetermined as to its cause.' So: skeptical of the leading version, agnostic about the general claim. Watch for answers that push the author to either pole.

choices.note: Too strong. The author criticizes the versions of early dark energy, but leaves the cause 'undetermined'. That isn't rejection.
The trap. This is exactly the reasoning paragraph 4 calls 'premature': the Cepheid result surviving 'does not show that the ladder as a whole is sound.'
Wrong on two counts: the author clearly cares, and expects observation (standard sirens) to settle it once 'such measurements mature.'
The author predicts no outcome; sirens 'promise such a determination' without favoring either value.
CORRECT. 'Reserved judgment' = 'premature' and 'undetermined as to its cause'; 'skepticism about the most prominent version' = early dark energy as 'less a prediction than an accommodation.'

questions.stem: Two survey teams measure the width of a canyon by chains of triangulation that begin from the same baseline but pass through different intermediate landmarks, and their results persistently disagree. Based on the passage, which one of the following would be most analogous to the kind of determination that the author says the debate over the Hubble constant most needs?
choices: timing a laser pulse reflected from the far rim, which relies on neither the baseline nor any landmark
having the first team repeat its survey with more precise instruments at each of its intermediate landmarks
running a third chain of triangulation from the same baseline through yet another set of intermediate landmarks
averaging the two teams' results, giving each a weight that reflects the uncertainty the team has stated
having the second team recalibrate its intermediate landmarks against the positions measured by the first team
questions.explanation: The author wants 'not a further refinement of either rung but a determination of the constant that shares none of the ladder's assumptions' (paragraph 4, third sentence), like sirens whose distances 'follow from general relativity rather than from any stellar calibration.' A laser timing that uses neither the baseline nor the landmarks is the counterpart. B is 'refinement of either rung'; C shares the baseline, just as both ladders share their supernovae.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Map the scenario onto the passage, then find the counterpart of the measurement the author wants.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second through fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Map it out: shared baseline = what the two ladder calibrations hold in common (the same supernovae); different intermediate landmarks = Cepheid vs. red-giant rungs; persistent disagreement = the persistent disagreement between the two calibrations. The author rejects 'further refinement of either rung' and asks for a determination that 'shares none of the ladder's assumptions.' So the right answer must avoid both the baseline and the landmarks.

choices.note: CORRECT. Shares nothing with either chain, just as sirens' distances 'follow from general relativity rather than from any stellar calibration.'
This is 'a further refinement of either rung', which the author explicitly says is not what the debate needs, much like the JWST re-observation of Cepheids.
The tempting near miss: a new rung, like the red-giant calibration, but it still shares the baseline, so it doesn't share 'none of the ladder's assumptions.'
Combining the existing results adds no independent information and can't tell which chain has the error.
Ties one method to the other's assumptions, the opposite of independence.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the author's claim in the fourth paragraph that the ladder's error budget does not yet capture all of its systematic uncertainty?
choices: A second, independent team analyzing the James Webb observations of distant Cepheids has obtained the same measurements as the first.
Versions of early dark energy have been devised that do not worsen agreement with measurements of how matter has clustered.
Several groups using the red-giant method have obtained values that differ from one another by more than their stated uncertainties.
The Cepheid-based and red-giant-based values differ by no more than chance would be expected to produce, given their stated uncertainties.
The gravitational-wave measurements reported so far are consistent both with the microwave-background value and with the distance-ladder value.
questions.explanation: The author's only evidence for the claim is 'the persistent disagreement between Cepheid-based and red-giant-based calibrations' (paragraph 4, second sentence). If that difference is within what the stated uncertainties allow by chance, it no longer shows any uncounted systematic error: D. C strengthens the claim, and A addresses the Cepheid photometry, which the author already grants is sound.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages the evidence for the author's claim about the ladder's error budget.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second sentence; paragraph 3, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Isolate the argument: premise, Cepheid-based and red-giant-based calibrations (sharing supernovae) persistently disagree; conclusion, the error budget misses some systematic uncertainty. The inference works only if the disagreement exceeds what the stated uncertainties can account for. Attack that link. Ignore answers about the other explanation (early dark energy) or about things the author already concedes.

choices.note: The author already accepts that 'the Cepheid measurements survive scrutiny' and argues the ladder could still be unsound. Confirming the Cepheids again doesn't touch the claim.
Concerns the new-physics explanation, not the ladder's error budget. It might make new physics more plausible, but it doesn't show the error budget is complete.
Strengthens the claim. Scatter beyond stated uncertainties is evidence of unaccounted systematics.
CORRECT. If the disagreement is within the range chance would produce, it is no evidence that the error budget misses anything, and it is the author's only evidence.
Consistent with the passage ('too loosely to adjudicate') and irrelevant to whether the ladder's stated uncertainties are complete.

questions.stem: The passage cites each of the following as grounds for caution about one of the explanations of the disagreement discussed in the second paragraph EXCEPT:
choices: Proposed forms of early dark energy tend to worsen agreement with measurements of how matter has clustered.
Gravitational-wave standard sirens have so far yielded values closer to the microwave-background estimate than to the ladder's.
Early dark energy must be made to operate only during the period in which it would most reduce the discrepancy.
Infrared images of distant Cepheids, in which crowding is largely resolved, closely match the earlier measurements of those stars.
Calibrations of the distance ladder that are based on different kinds of stars continue to disagree with one another.
questions.explanation: The passage says only that the siren events so far 'constrain the constant too loosely to adjudicate between the competing values' (paragraph 4); it never says they favor either value, so B is not cited as grounds for caution about anything. A and C are paragraph 3's objections to early dark energy, D is the JWST result against the crowding hypothesis, and E is paragraph 4's reason for doubting that the discrepancy 'must therefore reflect new physics.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one choice the passage does not offer as grounds for caution about either explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second and third sentences; paragraph 4, first, second and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: List the passage's grounds for caution. Against early dark energy: it worsens clustering fits; it must be tuned to a particular epoch. Against Cepheid systematic error: JWST resolves the crowding and reproduces the old measurements. Against concluding new physics: the persistent Cepheid/red-giant disagreement. Sirens are mentioned only as a future test whose current data are too loose to decide anything.

choices.note: Cited: paragraph 3, 'tend to worsen agreement with measurements of how matter has clustered.'
CORRECT. Not cited, and inconsistent with the passage: sirens 'constrain the constant too loosely to adjudicate between the competing values.'
Cited: early dark energy 'must be tuned to switch on and off at precisely the epoch at which they would do the most good.'
Cited: JWST's 'sharper infrared images largely resolve the crowding' and 'closely reproduced the earlier Cepheid measurements.'
Cited: paragraph 4 uses the 'persistent disagreement between Cepheid-based and red-giant-based calibrations' to show it is 'premature' to conclude the discrepancy must reflect new physics.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Snyder and Cohen's reconstruction shows that the reflexivity Foucault and Searle attributed to Las Meninas is an illusion produced by inattentive viewing rather than by anything in the painting.
Foucault's account of Las Meninas, unlike Searle's, survives Snyder and Cohen's correction because it concerns the viewer's experience rather than the painting's structure.
Snyder and Cohen's geometry defeats Searle's paradox, but the reflexive effect critics find in Las Meninas is real, arising from a misperception the painting is built to induce.
Las Meninas deliberately violates the conventions of illusionistic painting in order to make its viewers aware of their own place in the act of representation.
Because geometric analysis cannot capture how a painting is experienced, reconstructions of perspective are of little use in interpreting Las Meninas.
questions.explanation: The author accepts Snyder and Cohen's geometry and agrees it removes Searle's paradox (paragraph 4, sentence 1), but denies that the reflexivity is 'merely an illusion' (sentence 2): the painting 'reliably induces an error' that Velázquez built in. C states both halves. A is Snyder and Cohen's own conclusion, the one the author rejects; B misplaces Foucault, who located the void in the painting, not in the viewer.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the author's overall thesis, including both what the author accepts and what the author adds.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraphs 4 and 5, where the author speaks in the first person.

breakdown.analysis: Three views (Foucault, Searle, Snyder and Cohen), then the author: 'On the geometry I believe Snyder and Cohen are right' + 'It does not follow, however, that the reflexivity... is merely an illusion.' The main point must carry the concession and the refinement. Answers that give only one side, or that hand the thesis to one of the critics, are traps.

choices.note: This is Snyder and Cohen's conclusion as the author describes it ('merely an illusion that measurement dispels'), which the author explicitly says 'does not follow.' The most attractive wrong answer for a reader who stops after paragraph 3.

The author says Foucault 'described the experience... more faithfully than he explained it,' because Foucault located the void in the picture; the author does not say Foucault's account concerns the viewer or survives intact. Misattribution.

CORRECT. Paragraph 4: Snyder and Cohen are 'right' and dispose of Searle's paradox; yet the reflexivity is not 'merely an illusion,' since the picture 'reliably induces an error' that is 'too predictable to be an accident.' Paragraph 5 joins the two.
This is Searle's view ('violates the very conventions on which it depends'), which the author rejects: the depicted space is 'wholly coherent.'
Too strong. The author calls Snyder and Cohen 'right' on the geometry and says a satisfactory account must 'join' that geometry to an account of looking. Geometry is insufficient, not useless.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Any misreading of a painting that most of its viewers share must have been intended by the painter.
Las Meninas contains an inconsistency in its depicted space that Velázquez introduced in order to provoke reflection on representation.
Snyder and Cohen's reconstruction of the room's perspective is less reliable than viewers' immediate impressions of the scene.
Foucault's interpretation of Las Meninas is preferable to Snyder and Cohen's because Foucault attends to the experience of viewers.
A critic can describe a painting's effect on viewers accurately while misidentifying its cause.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says Foucault 'described the experience of the picture more faithfully than he explained it': his description of the void is faithful, but he wrongly located it in the depicted space. That is E in general terms. A overgeneralizes the author's claim about this one misreading ('too predictable to be an accident'); D ranks Foucault above Snyder and Cohen, which the author never does.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's views support, often stated more generally than the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, last two sentences; paragraph 5, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author's two commitments: (1) the painting's space is coherent (Snyder and Cohen are right); (2) the reflexive experience is real and designed. From these the author judges Foucault: right about the experience, wrong about its source. Prephrase: a description of an effect can be right while its explanation is wrong. Beware generalizations that go beyond 'this misreading.'

choices.note: Too strong. The author argues that this particular misreading is 'too predictable to be an accident of reception' given where Velázquez placed the mirror. Nothing commits the author to the claim that every shared misreading is intended.
Opposite. The author calls the depicted space 'wholly coherent'; the effect comes from the viewer's error, not from an inconsistency in the picture.
The author accepts the reconstruction ('On the geometry I believe Snyder and Cohen are right') and calls viewers' impression an 'error.'

The author never ranks the two. The author faults Foucault's explanation and Snyder and Cohen's inference, and calls for joining Snyder and Cohen's geometry to an account of looking. Half right at most.

CORRECT. Foucault 'described the experience of the picture more faithfully than he explained it': the effect he describes is real, but 'the void he found is not a feature of the depicted space,' as his explanation assumed.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: Searle's paradox depends on an assumption about what the mirror in Las Meninas reflects.
Snyder and Cohen denied that the king and queen are among the subjects depicted anywhere in Las Meninas.
Foucault's analysis was offered in part as a response to the puzzle that Searle had identified.
Snyder and Cohen held that most viewers correctly perceive what the mirror in Las Meninas reflects.
Searle maintained that Las Meninas fails as a work of art because it violates the conventions of illusionistic painting.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that 'once the reflection is understood as an image of a painted image, nothing obliges us to suppose that the picture is painted from the couple's place, and Searle's paradox dissolves.' A change in what we take the mirror to reflect removes the paradox, so the paradox depends on an assumption about the reflection. C is ruled out by the dates (Foucault 1966, Searle 1980); D attributes to Snyder and Cohen a view about viewers that the passage gives only to the author.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim the passage's statements best support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (Searle) and paragraph 3, especially its fourth sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Searle's puzzle needs the picture to be painted 'from the place of the royal couple.' What made that seem so? The mirror appearing to show them standing where we stand. Snyder and Cohen's move is to reinterpret the reflection, and with it the paradox 'dissolves.' So the paradox rests on a reading of the mirror. Check each trap against dates and against who says what.

choices.note: CORRECT. Reinterpreting the reflection as 'an image of a painted image' is enough to make 'Searle's paradox dissolve' (paragraph 3, sentence 4). The paradox therefore rests on an assumption about what the mirror reflects.
Opposite. Snyder and Cohen hold that the large canvas 'therefore depicts the king and queen'; the couple are depicted, on the canvas within the picture and in its reflection.
Chronology rules it out: Foucault's analysis is from 1966 and Searle's from 1980. Foucault cannot have been responding to Searle.

The passage never reports Snyder and Cohen's view of how viewers perceive the mirror; the claim that 'almost every viewer' errs is the author's, drawn from their analysis. If anything, the author's reading implies viewers err.
Searle says the work 'violates the very conventions on which it depends,' a claim about its logic, not a verdict that it fails as art. Out of scope.

questions.stem: The author's remark that a contradiction depending on a misplaced vanishing point "is a contradiction in the beholder's report, not in the picture" (first sentence of the fourth paragraph) functions primarily to
choices: concede that the reflexivity critics have found in Las Meninas exists only in their descriptions of the painting
explain why the author takes Snyder and Cohen's correction to dispose of Searle's paradox completely
suggest that Searle's account of the rule governing illusionistic pictures is mistaken
indicate that the author's disagreement with Snyder and Cohen concerns their reconstruction of the room's perspective
anticipate an objection to the author's claim that the painting reliably induces an error in its viewers
questions.explanation: The remark follows a colon after the claim that Snyder and Cohen's correction 'disposes of Searle's paradox more completely than his defenders have conceded.' It gives the reason: if the contradiction comes from misplacing the vanishing point, it was never in the picture, so nothing of it survives. A is the trap: the next sentence denies that the reflexivity is 'merely an illusion.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify why the author makes this remark at this point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentence 1: the clause before the colon and the one after.

breakdown.analysis: A colon often introduces a justification. Before it: the correction disposes of the paradox 'more completely than his defenders have conceded.' After it: the contradiction was in Searle's report, not in the painting. So the remark justifies the 'completely.' Don't confuse Searle's paradox (which the author rejects entirely) with reflexivity (which the author keeps).

choices.note: Trap. The remark concerns Searle's contradiction, not reflexivity in general, and the very next sentence denies that the reflexivity 'is merely an illusion.' Right idea, wrong target.

CORRECT. The remark, introduced by a colon, gives the reason the correction disposes of the paradox 'more completely than his defenders have conceded': the contradiction was never in the picture at all.
The author doesn't dispute Searle's rule; the error was factual (a 'misplaced vanishing point'), not a mistake about conventions.
Opposite. The author says 'On the geometry I believe Snyder and Cohen are right'; the disagreement concerns what follows from the geometry.
The claim about an induced error comes in the third sentence, after this remark, and the remark raises no objection to it.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Snyder and Cohen's analysis can most accurately be described as
choices: unreserved endorsement of both its reconstruction of the painting's geometry and its conclusion about the painting's reflexivity
doubt about its reconstruction of the painting's geometry combined with sympathy for its rejection of Searle's paradox
respect for its rigor tempered by the view that it addresses a question irrelevant to the painting's meaning
acceptance of its account of the painting's space but not of what it takes that account to show about reflexivity
qualified approval, on the grounds that it corrects Searle's error about the painting but commits the same error in a different form
questions.explanation: The author accepts the geometry ('On the geometry I believe Snyder and Cohen are right') but rejects the inference they 'seem to conclude' from it, that the reflexivity is 'merely an illusion that measurement dispels.' D captures that split. B reverses it: the author has no doubt about the geometry.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's stance toward Snyder and Cohen, precisely.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first two sentences; paragraph 5, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Two separate parts of Snyder and Cohen's work: the geometry (accepted fully) and the conclusion drawn about reflexivity (rejected: 'It does not follow'). The right answer splits along that line. Watch for answers that split along a different line or reverse the halves.

choices.note: Too strong. The author rejects their apparent conclusion that the reflexivity is 'merely an illusion.'
Reversed. The author accepts the geometry without reservation; the reservation concerns the conclusion drawn from it.
