The author does not call the geometry irrelevant; a satisfactory account 'must... join the geometry that Snyder and Cohen supplied' to an account of looking.
CORRECT. Accepts the geometry ('right'), disagrees that it shows the reflexivity is an illusion ('It does not follow, however...').
The author never says Snyder and Cohen repeat Searle's error. Their mistake is an unwarranted inference, not a misplaced vanishing point.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A feature of a painting is said to invite competing accounts; two reflexive readings are summarized; a third, rejecting a premise of one, is presented; the author accepts that rejection but disputes an inference drawn from it and proposes a synthesis.

A painting is described; three interpretations of it are summarized in the order in which they appeared; the author then argues that the earliest of the three interpretations is correct and that the two later ones rest on misunderstandings of it.

A puzzle about a painting is posed; two attempts to solve the puzzle are presented and found wanting; the author then offers a new solution that rejects an assumption shared by every earlier account of the painting.

A painting is described; two interpretations of it are criticized on the basis of a third; the author then defends the third interpretation against an objection that proponents of the first two would be likely to raise.

Three interpretations of a painting are summarized; the author identifies a factual error common to all three and concludes that the meaning of the painting cannot be determined by examining its geometry.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes the mirror and gazes and announces three accounts; paragraph 2 gives Foucault and Searle, both reading the picture as reflexive; paragraph 3 gives Snyder and Cohen, who reject Searle's factual premise; paragraphs 4-5 accept that correction, deny that it shows reflexivity is an illusion, and call for joining geometry with an account of looking. That is A. D is the near miss: the author does not defend the third account but disputes its conclusion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the sequence of the passage's moves.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of each paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1 setup (mirror, outward gazes, 'three accounts'); P2 Foucault + Searle; P3 Snyder and Cohen against Searle; P4 author: right on geometry, wrong inference; P5 author's synthesis. Test each choice step by step; one wrong step eliminates it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Each clause matches: the feature (mirror and gazes, P1); two reflexive accounts (Foucault, Searle, P2); a third rejecting Searle's premise (P3); acceptance plus 'It does not follow' (P4); the combined account (P5).
The author does not say Foucault is correct (he 'explained' the experience wrongly), and the later accounts don't depend on misunderstanding Foucault.
The author's account isn't a new solution to Searle's puzzle (the author accepts Snyder and Cohen's solution), and Snyder and Cohen's attempt is not 'found wanting' as a solution.
Snyder and Cohen criticize only Searle, and the author doesn't defend them against an objection; the author objects to their conclusion.
No error common to all three is identified (Snyder and Cohen are 'right' on geometry), and the author holds that geometry is necessary, not useless.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the role the author attributes to the mirror in Las Meninas?
choices: A painting admired as an old master is shown by chemical analysis to be a later copy, after which critics agree that the admiration rested on nothing in the work itself.
A mystery novel's narrator misleads readers about the culprit throughout and then confesses the deception in the last chapter, so every reader who finishes the book learns the truth.
A textbook diagram leads nearly all readers to misjudge the relative lengths of two lines, an effect later traced to a printing error that the diagram's designer did not foresee.
A world map visibly enlarges regions near the poles, a distortion that its makers explain in a legend so that readers can correct for it while consulting the map.
A colonnade built to shrink toward its far end reliably looks far deeper than it is; only measurement reveals its length, and that illusion is what its builder meant.
questions.explanation: The author's mirror has four features: its space is coherent, viewers reliably misread it, only a reconstruction no one performs while looking corrects the misreading, and the misreading was designed. The colonnade (E) has all four. B fails because the correction is built into the experience of the work itself; C fails on design (the error was unforeseen); A has no designed effect and draws the dismissive conclusion the author rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation with the same structure as the author's account of the mirror.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 3-5.

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the author's view: (1) nothing actually inconsistent; (2) a predictable misperception; (3) corrected only by measurement outside the act of looking; (4) the misperception is the maker's intended effect. Look for all four. Each wrong answer drops one.

choices.note: Mirrors Snyder and Cohen's 'measurement dispels it' conclusion, which the author rejects, and nothing indicates the error was designed into the work as an experience for its viewers.

Strong trap: a designed, predictable misleading. But the correction is delivered inside the work to every reader, whereas in Las Meninas 'only a reconstruction no one performs while looking can correct it.'
Predictable error, but an accident the designer 'did not foresee'; the author insists the mirror's misreading is 'too predictable to be an accident.'
No misperception is induced: the distortion is disclosed and corrected in use.

CORRECT. Coherent structure, reliable misperception, correction only by measurement, and the illusion is what the builder 'meant,' just as Velázquez 'set the reflection exactly where the eye would most readily mistake it.'

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: whether democracies are in general less inclined than other states to go to war
whether the rarity of war between democracies results from their being democracies
how the relative importance of institutional constraints and democratic norms should be assessed
whether the pattern of peace between democracies held before the First World War
whether governments should promote democracy abroad as a means of reducing war
questions.explanation: Passage A asks 'whether something other than regime type produces the pattern' and argues that a residual effect of democracy survives; passage B accepts the pattern and asks 'what the fact shows,' arguing that shared interests may explain it. Both concern whether democracy causes the peace (B). E is the main trap: both passages end by touching on promoting democracy, but neither argues for or against a policy.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the topic both passages are mainly about.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 2, sentence 1; passage B, paragraph 1, sentence 1.

breakdown.analysis: Both accept that democracies rarely fight one another. The issue between them is the source: regime type (A) or shared interests that coincided with democracy after 1945 (B). The answer must fit both; eliminate topics only one passage develops or that each mentions only at the end.

choices.note: Passage A raises this in one sentence only to say democracies are not generally less warlike; passage B doesn't discuss it.
CORRECT. A: 'whether something other than regime type produces the pattern'; B: the fact is not in dispute, 'what the fact shows is.'
Only passage A discusses the two mechanisms, and only briefly ('Their relative weight remains unsettled').
Only passage B discusses the period before 1914.
Tempting because both passages end near this point, but A only expects fewer wars and B only notes what such policies 'rest on.' Neither is primarily about the policy question.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: pairs of democracies have only rarely fought wars against each other
accountability to voters can make leaders reluctant to go to war
democracies fight nondemocracies about as often as other states do
the statistical record warrants expecting that more democracies will mean fewer wars among them
shared interests between two states can by themselves reduce the likelihood that the two will fight
questions.explanation: Passage A concludes that the persistent association 'warrants the expectation that a world containing more democracies will see fewer wars among them'; passage B says that question is one the record 'cannot settle' and that such expectations 'rest on an answer the evidence does not yet supply.' A, B, and E are points they share; C is something passage B never addresses.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim one author would affirm and the other deny.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of each passage.

breakdown.analysis: These authors agree on a lot: the pattern exists (B: 'not in dispute'), democratic dispositions may restrain leaders (B concedes), and shared interests reduce conflict (A lists alliance ties). The real split is inferential: does the evidence license the forward-looking expectation? A yes, B not yet.

choices.note: Both accept this. B: 'That pairs of democracies have rarely fought one another is not in dispute.'
Both accept it: A gives it as a mechanism; B concedes accountability 'may well make democratic leaders slower to fight.'
Only A states this; B is silent, so no disagreement can be inferred.

CORRECT. A: the association 'warrants the expectation' of fewer wars; B: the record 'cannot settle' whether democratic dispositions would suffice, and the expectation rests on 'an answer the evidence does not yet supply.'
Both accept it: A lists alliance ties as something that 'may independently reduce the risk of conflict'; B's whole argument relies on it.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to agree that
choices: the absence of war between democracies before 1914 was largely a matter of chance
controlling for formal alliance membership adequately captures the shared interests of states
factors other than democracy may account for some of the observed peace between democracies
institutional constraints on leaders do more than democratic norms to keep democracies at peace with one another
the peace between democracies would survive a divergence in the interests that bind them together
questions.explanation: Passage A says that under controls the effect of joint democracy 'shrinks without disappearing,' so 'some of the raw association... belongs to democracy's companions'; passage B attributes the post-1945 peace in part to shared opposition to the Soviet Union. Both therefore accept C. B is A's apparent view that B explicitly rejects; E is A-leaning and is exactly what B says is unsettled.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim both authors would accept.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 2, sentences 3-4; passage B, paragraph 1.

breakdown.analysis: A seems to defend democracy as cause and B to attack it, but A concedes part of the association is due to wealth, alliances, distance, and B concedes democracy may matter. The overlap: other factors account for at least some of the peace. A hedged answer ('some... may') is likely the key.

choices.note: Neither says this. B reports that democratic pairs were not less likely to have disputes before 1914, not that the lack of war was chance; A doesn't discuss the period.
B rejects it: 'Controlling for formal alliances does not resolve the difficulty.'
CORRECT. A: 'Some of the raw association... belongs to democracy's companions'; B: allies against a common adversary 'have compelling reasons not to fight one another whatever their constitutions.'
A says the relative weight 'remains unsettled'; B doesn't compare the mechanisms.
B says this 'cannot' yet be settled; A's expectation doesn't speak to divergent interests directly. Not a shared view.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage A but not in passage B?
choices: the possibility that leaders accountable to voters are reluctant to fight
the role of a common adversary in discouraging conflict among allied states
a distinction between hostilities in general and hostilities that count as war
the expectation that an increase in the number of democracies would reduce war
the possibility that geographic distance reduces conflict
questions.explanation: Passage A lists 'geographic distance' among factors that 'may independently reduce the risk of conflict'; passage B never mentions distance. A, C, and D appear in both passages (B's 'Accountability to electorates,' 'militarized disputes... escalated to war,' and 'policies that promote democracy abroad in the expectation of peace'); B appears only in passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find an item present in A and absent from B.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 2, sentence 2.

breakdown.analysis: Check each choice twice: is it in A? is it in B? Most traps are in both, worded differently in each. The common adversary is B's alone.

choices.note: In both: A's 'leaders answerable to voters'; B's 'Accountability to electorates.'
Reversed: only passage B mentions the Soviet Union as a common adversary.
In both: A's 'hostilities too limited to count as war'; B's disputes that never 'escalated to war.'
In both: A's 'expectation that a world containing more democracies will see fewer wars'; B's policies adopted 'in the expectation of peace.'
CORRECT. Only A mentions 'geographic distance' as a factor that may reduce conflict.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to say which one of the following about the studies described in the third sentence of the second paragraph of passage A?
choices: The effect that remains in them could still reflect shared interests not expressed in formal alliances.
Those studies in fact show that democracy has no independent effect on the likelihood of war between states.
Those studies err chiefly in relying on data drawn from the period before the First World War.
Those studies exaggerate the extent to which geographic distance reduces the risk of conflict.
The results of those studies would be decisive if they examined militarized disputes as well as wars.
questions.explanation: Passage A's studies control for wealth, alliance ties, and distance and find a residual effect. Passage B says 'controlling for formal alliances does not resolve the difficulty, because common interests extend well beyond treaty commitments.' So B would say the residual could still reflect uncoded shared interests (A). B is too strong: B says its argument does not show 'that democracy is irrelevant to peace.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply passage B's view to passage A's control studies.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 2, sentence 3; passage B, paragraph 1, last two sentences, and paragraph 2, sentence 1.

breakdown.analysis: A: controls shrink but do not eliminate the effect. B: alliance controls miss interests that no one 'could code.' Prephrase: the leftover effect may not be democracy's at all. The hedge 'could still' matches B's cautious stance.

choices.note: CORRECT. B: alliance controls do 'not resolve the difficulty, because common interests extend well beyond treaty commitments.' The residual could be those uncoded interests.
Too strong. B: 'None of this shows that democracy is irrelevant to peace,' and Farber and Gowa 'did not claim that it does.'
Nothing indicates the studies' period, and B's concern is post-1945 interests, not pre-1914 data.
B never discusses distance.
B never suggests that adding disputes would make the results decisive; B's objection, the uncontrolled shared interests, would remain.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the position taken by the author of passage B?
choices: During the Cold War, nondemocratic states aligned with the Western democracies seldom engaged in militarized disputes with one another or with their democratic allies.
Before the First World War, relatively few states met the criteria for democracy used in most statistical studies.
Voters in democracies frequently support wars at their outset and withdraw support only as casualties mount.
Since the Cold War ended, democratic pairs with sharply divergent foreign-policy interests have been no more prone to militarized disputes than closely aligned democratic pairs.
During the Cold War, democracies fought wars against nondemocracies about as often as nondemocracies fought wars against one another.
questions.explanation: B's position is that the post-1945 peace may reflect shared interests, and that whether democratic dispositions would keep the peace 'once the interests that bound them together diverged' is unsettled. D supplies evidence from outside the single era B criticizes: democracies with divergent interests remain as peaceful with each other as aligned ones, so interests aren't doing the work. A supports B by showing aligned nondemocracies also kept the peace.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages passage B's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, paragraph 1, sentences 4-5, and paragraph 2, sentences 3-4.

breakdown.analysis: B's argument: post-1945 data confound institutions with interests, so they can't show democracy alone keeps the peace. To undermine it, separate the two variables: democracies without shared interests that still keep the peace. Avoid answers that support B or that bear on passage A's mechanisms only.

choices.note: Strengthens B: aligned states keep the peace whatever their regime, as B's interest explanation predicts.
Consistent with B and, if anything, explains why the pre-1914 evidence is thin; it doesn't touch B's argument about post-1945 interests.
Cuts against one of A's proposed mechanisms, and so if anything weakens the case B is questioning; it doesn't undermine B.
CORRECT. Divergent-interest democratic pairs are no more dispute-prone than aligned ones: the peace survives the divergence B said the evidence could not yet address, and interests can't explain it.
About wars between democracies and nondemocracies; B's argument concerns peace within democratic pairs. Irrelevant.

questions.stem: By "The peace is a property of the pair, not of the regime" (last sentence of the first paragraph of passage A), the author of passage A most probably means that
choices: the absence of war between two democracies depends on their being roughly equal in military strength
whether a democracy remains at peace depends more on the policies of its current government than on its constitution
democracies are less likely to fight one another, though not less likely to fight in general
peace between democracies results from the alliances they form rather than from their political institutions
the effect has been detected only by studies that examine pairs of states rather than individual states
questions.explanation: The preceding sentence says democracies 'are not in general less warlike than other states; they fight nondemocracies about as often as other states do.' So the peace attaches to democratic pairs, not to democracy as a feature of a single state (C). E reads the phrase as a claim about research method; D gives passage B's explanation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Determine what the quoted sentence means in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 1, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence summarizes the one before it: democracies fight nondemocracies as much as anyone; they just don't fight each other. 'Pair' = dyad of two democracies; 'regime' = the type of government of one state. Prephrase: the peace shows up only between democracies.

choices.note: Military parity is never mentioned; 'pair' means two democracies, not two equal states.
Reads 'regime' as 'current government.' The passage is contrasting democracy as a property of one state with a property of two democratic states.
CORRECT. Right after saying democracies are 'not in general less warlike' and fight nondemocracies 'about as often,' the author concludes the peace belongs to democratic pairs.
This is passage B's alternative explanation. Passage A attributes the peace to joint democracy, with alliances as one control.
Tempting because 'pair' sounds methodological, but the sentence summarizes a fact about how democracies behave, not about how studies are designed.

questions.stimulus:
Moreno: The journal's new policy of publishing replication studies whatever their outcome will probably make it less prestigious, and I admit that worries me. But a journal's standing ought to rest on the reliability of what it prints, and failed replications tell readers which earlier findings deserve less of their trust. So the policy is worth what it costs.

Achebe: I agree that reliability should count for more than prestige, and that a well-conducted failed replication is valuable information. But careless replication attempts are far more likely to fail than careful ones, and a journal committed to publishing replications whatever their outcome will attract a flood of careless failures. Readers cannot easily tell those apart from careful ones, so the policy will lead them to doubt sound findings for no good reason, leaving them worse placed than before to know what to believe.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Moreno and Achebe disagree over whether
choices: the reliability of what a journal publishes should matter more to it than its prestige
the journal's new policy will lower the journal's prestige
a well-conducted replication study that fails to reproduce an earlier finding gives readers useful information about how far to trust that earlier finding
the journal's new policy will, on balance, improve readers' ability to tell which published findings deserve their trust
the journal should publish replication studies at all
questions.explanation: Each speaker concedes the other's background points. Achebe grants that reliability outranks prestige and that good failed replications are informative, and Moreno grants that prestige may suffer. The live issue is the policy's net effect on readers: Moreno says it tells them which findings to trust less, and Achebe says it leaves them "worse placed than before" to know what to believe, (D). (A) and (C) are stated agreements, and (E) overstates Achebe's objection.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Moreno: The outcome-blind replication policy may cost prestige, but failed replications tell readers what to trust less, so it's worth it.; Achebe: Agreed that reliability matters most and that good failed replications help, but the policy will attract careless failures that readers can't distinguish, leaving them worse off.

breakdown.analysis: List the concessions first, because they eliminate answers. Achebe concedes reliability > prestige and the value of well-done failed replications. Moreno concedes the prestige hit and isn't contradicted on it. What's left? Moreno's reason the policy is worth it is that readers learn which findings to trust less. Achebe's whole reply attacks exactly that: on balance, readers end up worse at knowing what to believe. That is the disagreement, and it's about the policy's effect on readers, not about prestige or the value of replication.

choices.note: Both agree. Moreno says standing "ought to rest on reliability"; Achebe says "I agree that reliability should count for more than prestige."
Moreno thinks so; Achebe never addresses prestige effects. Only one speaker has a view.
Both agree. Achebe explicitly grants that a well-conducted failed replication is valuable information, and Moreno's argument rests on it.
CORRECT. Moreno: yes, failed replications tell readers what to trust less, so the policy is worth it. Achebe: no, readers will doubt sound findings and be "worse placed than before."

The near-miss. Moreno favors publishing them, but Achebe objects only to publishing them whatever their outcome, which brings in careless work. Nothing he says opposes publishing careful replications.

questions.stimulus: When the city of Pellam eliminated bus fares last year, transit officials expected the change to benefit chiefly its lower-income residents, most of whom had told surveyors the year before that the cost of fares was their main reason for not riding the bus more often. Officials announced the change months in advance through notices on buses, at stops, and in local newspapers. Yet a year after the change, the number of bus trips taken by lower-income residents had risen by only 4 percent, while the number taken by higher-income residents, few of whom had ever cited fares as a deterrent, had risen by 30 percent. Throughout the year, the city ran the same routes on the same schedules, using the same number of buses, as it had before fares were eliminated.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: Most of the jobs held by Pellam's lower-income residents are in industrial areas on the city's outskirts that no bus route reaches.

Before fares were eliminated, buses serving Pellam's lower-income neighborhoods were already so full at peak hours that they often passed waiting riders, whereas buses serving higher-income neighborhoods ran with many empty seats.
At the same time that fares were eliminated, Pellam doubled its downtown parking fees, which are paid mainly by higher-income commuters who had previously driven to work.
A survey taken six months after the change found that nearly all of Pellam's lower-income residents knew that bus fares had been eliminated.
Most of the trips that Pellam's lower-income residents most often need to make occur late at night, when the city's buses run only once an hour.
questions.explanation: The puzzle: the group that said fares held it back barely rode more, while the group that didn't care about fares rode much more. (A), (B), and (E) show that something other than cost, with service unchanged, kept lower-income riders off the bus; (C) gives higher-income riders a new reason to ride. (D) only rules out one explanation (people didn't know), which makes the puzzle harder, not easier.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Lower-income residents named fares as the main barrier, yet after fares were eliminated their trips rose only 4 percent, while higher-income trips, never held back by fares, rose 30 percent.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: The change was widely announced; routes, schedules, and the number of buses stayed the same.

breakdown.analysis: Resolvers can work on either side: show why lower-income riding stayed flat (a barrier other than cost that free fares don't remove, especially given that service didn't expand), or why higher-income riding jumped (a new incentive). The odd one out will leave both sides as puzzling as before, or more so. Note the stimulus already hints at one non-resolver: awareness.

choices.note: If the jobs lower-income residents travel to aren't on any route, free fares can't make the bus useful for those trips. Resolves.
Full buses that pass waiting riders cap how many more trips lower-income residents could take with unchanged service, while higher-income routes had room. Resolves.
Higher parking fees that started at the same time give higher-income drivers a new reason to switch to the bus. Explains their 30 percent rise. Resolves.
CORRECT. This is the one that doesn't help. Knowing that the buses were free removes a possible explanation (residents hadn't heard), so the small increase is even more puzzling.
If the trips they most need fall when buses run once an hour, and schedules didn't change, service rather than cost limits their riding. Resolves.

questions.stimulus: Council member: Our city has committed to cutting the volume of waste it sends to the landfill by a third within five years. The regional planning board's studies establish that no city of our size can achieve a reduction of that magnitude unless it collects food scraps at the curb; improvements to recycling alone have never come close. Opponents of the proposal before us object that it is costly and that participation in such programs typically starts slowly. I grant both points. A program that costs more than expected and grows slowly is regrettable, but neither fact is a reason to abandon a goal the council has already adopted. The proposal establishes precisely the kind of curbside food-scrap collection the board identified, and it does so citywide. So by adopting it we will put the city on course to meet its target, and the cost, whatever it turns out to be, is one we should accept.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the council member's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: rejects the opponents' objections on the grounds that those who raise them have reasons of their own for wanting the proposal defeated
takes a condition that the cited studies show must be met for the goal to be reached to be one whose fulfillment ensures that the goal will be reached
infers that a measure is required for reaching a goal from evidence showing only that the measure has been enough to reach that goal in other cities of comparable size
fails to consider that a program whose participation starts slowly might nonetheless grow enough over five years to meet the target
applies to its own city a finding about cities of a certain size without establishing that its city resembles those cities in other relevant respects
questions.explanation: The board's studies make curbside food-scrap collection necessary for a one-third cut ("no city ... can ... unless"). The council member concludes that adopting it will put the city on course to meet the target, treating the necessary condition as sufficient, (B). (C) is the reversed trap: it describes inferring necessity from sufficiency, but the necessity is given as a premise and the error runs the other way.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Adopting the curbside food-scrap proposal will put the city on course to meet its one-third reduction target, so its cost should be accepted.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: No city of this size can make a one-third cut unless it collects food scraps at the curb; the proposal creates exactly that collection. Opponents' points about cost and slow participation are conceded but set aside.

breakdown.analysis: The concession about cost and slow participation is a distraction: the council member answers it fairly by saying those points don't justify dropping the goal. The real move is buried in the "unless" sentence. "No city can cut a third unless it collects food scraps" means collection is required (cut → collection). The conclusion runs the arrow backwards: collection → on course to cut. Prephrase: it treats something needed for success as something that guarantees it. Watch the abstract wording: (B) and (C) both talk about "required" and "enough", and only one has the direction right.

choices.note: No such attack occurs. The council member grants the opponents' points and argues around them; their motives never come up.
CORRECT. The studies show collection is necessary ("unless"); the conclusion treats it as sufficient for being on course. That is the arrow reversed.

The near-miss. It names the right confusion in the wrong direction. The argument doesn't infer that collection is required; the board's studies state that. The faulty step goes from required to enough, not from enough to required.
This possibility would help the council member, not hurt the argument. Pointing out that a program might succeed despite a slow start is no criticism of an argument for adopting it.
The board's finding is about all cities of this size ("no city of our size can..."). Applying a universal claim to a member of the class it covers is valid; no further resemblance is needed.

questions.stimulus: Geologist: The boulders scattered across the Veska plain are made of a granite found nowhere within two hundred kilometers, so they must have been carried there. Three mechanisms could have done it: glaciers, floods, or deliberate transport by the plain's ancient inhabitants. Human transport can be set aside, since several of the boulders weigh more than any object known to have been moved by people of that era anywhere in the world. A flood powerful enough to move boulders of that size would also have scoured away the fine lake sediments beneath them, yet those sediments lie undisturbed. That leaves glaciers. Admittedly, no glacial scratches have been found on the plain's bedrock. But that bedrock is buried under several meters of the same lake sediments, and elsewhere in the region glacial scratches have been found only where bedrock is exposed at the surface. So the absence of observed scratches is no evidence against the glacial explanation, which we should accept.
questions.stem: The geologist's argument proceeds by
choices: showing that a widely accepted explanation of a phenomenon is inconsistent with evidence that its proponents have overlooked
ruling out all but one of a set of possible explanations and then arguing that a consideration that might seem to tell against the remaining explanation does not do so
using similarities between the plain and other sites in the region to establish that a phenomenon observed at those sites must also have occurred on the plain
ruling out all but one of a set of possible explanations and then presenting positive evidence, drawn from elsewhere in the region, that independently confirms the explanation that remains
arguing that because a certain kind of evidence has not been found, the explanation that such evidence would support should be rejected
questions.explanation: The geologist eliminates human transport and floods, leaving glaciers, and then defuses the apparent counterevidence (no scratches) by explaining why scratches wouldn't be visible even if glaciers were responsible: (B). (D) gets the elimination right but invents a second step. Explaining away the missing scratches is not positive evidence for glaciers.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Glaciers carried the boulders to the Veska plain.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Human transport is ruled out by weight and floods by the undisturbed sediments; the missing glacial scratches are explained by buried bedrock.

breakdown.analysis: This is a process of elimination with a defensive coda. Three candidates, two eliminated, and then "Admittedly..." introduces the strongest point against the survivor, which is neutralized rather than answered with new support. The regional comparison (scratches appear only on exposed bedrock) serves that neutralizing step; it doesn't prove glaciers came to Veska. So the right answer has two parts: elimination, then rebuttal of an objection.

choices.note: The geologist doesn't challenge an accepted explanation; she defends the one left standing.
CORRECT. Two of three explanations are eliminated, and the apparent problem for the third (no scratches) is shown not to count against it.
The regional sites are used only to show why scratches would be hidden at Veska, not to establish that glaciation occurred there.
The near-miss. The elimination is right, but nothing "independently confirms" glaciers. The second step removes an objection; it adds no support.
The reverse of what she argues. She says the missing scratches are no evidence against glaciers.

questions.stimulus: Retail analyst: Eighteen months ago the Bramble café chain introduced an order-ahead smartphone app at its forty city locations but not at its twenty suburban ones. Since then, average weekly revenue per city location has risen 14 percent, while revenue per suburban location has risen only 3 percent. The app evidently accounts for the difference. Before it existed, many city customers who arrived at peak hours abandoned long lines without buying anything; with the app, they can order in advance and simply collect their drinks when they arrive. Bramble's suburban locations also have lines at peak hours, so introducing the app at those locations should produce revenue gains comparable to the ones the chain's city locations have enjoyed over the past eighteen months, and Bramble's management, which is now weighing that expansion, should approve it.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the retail analyst's argument EXCEPT:
choices: In the year before the app was introduced, average weekly revenue had grown about 12 percent at Bramble's city locations and about 3 percent at its suburban ones.
Staff at Bramble's city locations recorded far fewer customers leaving lines without buying anything in the months after the app was introduced than in the months before it.
Peak-hour lines at Bramble's suburban locations are, on average, about as long as those at its city locations.
During the past eighteen months, Bramble made no change in prices, menu, or staffing at its city locations that it did not also make at its suburban locations.
Most of the increase in revenue at the city locations has come during the morning and midday hours, when lines are longest.
questions.explanation: Four choices support either the causal claim (the app caused the city-suburb gap) or the prediction (suburbs will gain similarly). (A) does the opposite: a 12-versus-3 gap already existed the year before the app, so most of the recent gap is a continuing trend, not the app's effect. That makes (A) the one that doesn't strengthen.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The app caused the city locations' larger revenue gain, and adding it in the suburbs should produce comparable gains.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: City revenue rose 14 percent with the app vs. 3 percent in the suburbs without it; the app lets peak-hour customers skip lines they used to abandon; suburbs have peak-hour lines too.

breakdown.analysis: There are two conclusions to support: a causal one and a prediction. Strengtheners can confirm the mechanism (fewer walkaways, gains at peak hours), rule out other causes (no other city-only changes), or show the suburbs are similar (lines as long). Look for the choice that does none of these, here one that offers a rival explanation for the gap. Run the numbers in each choice; one is buried there.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the one that doesn't strengthen. If the city locations were already outgrowing the suburbs by about 9 points a year before the app, most of the 11-point gap afterward is just the old trend continuing. That weakens the claim that the app caused it.
Fewer walkaways after the app is exactly the mechanism the analyst describes. Strengthens.
If suburban lines are as long as city ones, the app has as many lost sales to recover there. Strengthens the prediction.
This rules out other city-only changes that could have caused the gap. Strengthens the causal claim.
Gains concentrated in the hours with the longest lines fit the claim that the app works by letting people skip lines. Strengthens.

questions.stimulus: Education official: Two years ago, the Halden school district adopted the Stepwise curriculum for teaching fractions, while the neighboring Marrow district adopted the Visual curriculum. Since then, the share of Halden fifth-graders scoring proficient on the state fractions test has risen from 48 to 66 percent, whereas Marrow's share has risen only from 71 to 78 percent. Some have suggested that Halden's improvement merely reflects extra hiring, but student-teacher ratios in both districts were unchanged throughout the period. Both districts' students took the same state test each year, scored by the same independent agency, and the students in the two districts come from similar economic backgrounds. Clearly, then, the Stepwise curriculum is more effective at teaching fractions than the Visual curriculum is, and districts choosing between the two should adopt Stepwise.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the education official's argument?
choices: In each district, the newly adopted curriculum produced larger gains in proficiency than the curriculum it replaced had produced over a comparable period.
The state fractions test was revised last year to give greater weight to problems that involve visual models of fractions.
In surveys conducted last year, most parents in both districts rated their children's fractions instruction as satisfactory.
Halden's student-teacher ratio has for many years been somewhat higher than Marrow's.
Most Marrow fifth-graders who fail the state fractions test do so because of reading difficulties that neither curriculum addresses.
questions.explanation: The comparison rests on raw gains: 18 points in Halden versus 7 in Marrow. But Marrow started at 71 percent, so its remaining non-proficient students may be ones no fractions curriculum can reach. (E) says exactly that, so Marrow's small gain no longer shows that Visual is the weaker curriculum. (A) is the trap: it's about whether each curriculum works, not which works better.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Stepwise is more effective than Visual at teaching fractions; districts should adopt Stepwise.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Halden (Stepwise) rose 48 to 66 percent proficient; Marrow (Visual) rose only 71 to 78; staffing, test, scoring, and economic background were the same.

breakdown.analysis: The conclusion is comparative, so the right weakener has to undercut the comparison, not the curricula's effectiveness in general. The official ignores where each district started. Halden had 52 percent of students to lift; Marrow had only 29 percent, and those may be the hardest cases. Prephrase: something limits how much any fractions curriculum could raise Marrow's score, so the smaller gain isn't the curriculum's fault. Beware answers that only say both curricula helped.

choices.note: The near-miss. It says each curriculum beat its predecessor, which is about whether each one works. The conclusion is that Stepwise beats Visual, and this says nothing about that.
If the test shifted toward visual models, it would if anything favor Marrow's Visual-trained students, so Marrow's gain may be inflated. That helps the official.
Parent satisfaction is no measure of which curriculum teaches fractions better. Irrelevant.
The official's point is that ratios didn't change. A long-standing higher ratio in Halden would, if anything, make its larger gain more impressive. Doesn't weaken.

CORRECT. If most of Marrow's remaining failures stem from a reading problem neither curriculum touches, Marrow had little room for any fractions curriculum to improve. Its smaller gain then says nothing about Visual being less effective than Stepwise.

questions.stimulus: Art historian: Every surviving altarpiece from the Vell workshop was commissioned by a religious confraternity, and every one of them was paid for in full. Confraternity contracts in the region specified which pigments a painter could use, and any violation of a contract's terms cost the painter the entire payment. Contracts drawn up before 1550 invariably forbade imported ultramarine, insisting on cheaper local blues; of those drawn up from 1550 onward, roughly half permitted it. Chemical analysis has detected imported ultramarine in several Vell altarpieces. Admittedly, restorers in later centuries sometimes added ultramarine to old paintings, but in each of these several altarpieces the ultramarine lies beneath the original varnish, which has never been removed. The workshop's account books, which survive only for the years 1540 to 1555, record no purchases of ultramarine of any kind.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: At least some of the Vell workshop's surviving altarpieces were painted under contracts drawn up no earlier than 1550.
The Vell workshop bought imported ultramarine at some time after 1555.
No altarpiece painted by the Vell workshop before 1550 contains imported ultramarine.
Most of the Vell workshop's surviving altarpieces were painted under confraternity contracts that permitted the use of imported ultramarine.
Restorers never added imported ultramarine to any of the Vell workshop's altarpieces.
questions.explanation: Several Vell altarpieces have original ultramarine (it lies under the untouched original varnish). All were paid in full, so none broke its contract, so each of those contracts permitted ultramarine, and only contracts from 1550 onward ever did. So at least some were painted under contracts from 1550 or later: (A). (B) is the trap: the books show no purchase from 1540 to 1555, but the pigment could have been supplied by the confraternity.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: All surviving Vell altarpieces: confraternity commissions, paid in full. Violating a contract forfeited payment. Pre-1550 contracts banned imported ultramarine; about half from 1550 on allowed it. Several Vell altarpieces contain original ultramarine. Account books (1540 to 1555) show no ultramarine purchases.

breakdown.analysis: Chain the facts: original ultramarine, plus full payment, means the contract allowed it, which means the contract was from 1550 or later. That reaches 'several', no more. The traps will push past what the chain gives: to 'most', to 'no altarpiece ever', or to a claim about purchases that assumes the workshop had to buy the pigment itself. The modest answer is the one the chain reaches.

choices.note: CORRECT. The several altarpieces with original ultramarine were paid in full, so their contracts allowed it, and no contract before 1550 did. So at least those were painted under contracts from 1550 or later.
The near-miss. It assumes the workshop had to buy its own ultramarine. The confraternity that allowed the pigment could have supplied it, so the books' silence proves nothing about a later purchase.
Too broad. Restorers sometimes added ultramarine, and a pre-1550 Vell work (surviving or lost) could contain restorer-added pigment. The facts cover only the original paint in surviving works.
'Several' altarpieces with original ultramarine doesn't make most. We aren't told how many survive.
We know only that restorers didn't add the ultramarine in those several altarpieces. Restorers could have added it to others.

questions.stimulus:
Okafor: The ministry is right to rebuild the collapsed east wall of the Tessaly fortress. Visitors who see nothing but a jumble of fallen stones leave with no sense of what the fortress once was. And since the wall will be rebuilt from its own original stones, recovered from where they fell, the result will be as authentic as any visitor could reasonably ask.

Lindqvist: The stones are original, I grant you, and a bare field of rubble teaches visitors very little. But the authenticity of a structure is not simply a matter of what it is made of; it depends just as much on how those materials are arranged, and no record survives of how the stones of the east wall were laid. A wall rebuilt from guesswork will present a modern conjecture as if it were a medieval fact. Better a well-labeled field of rubble, honestly explained, than that.
questions.stem: Okafor and Lindqvist are committed to agreeing with which one of the following?
choices: The material from which the ministry proposes to rebuild the east wall is the material from which the wall was originally built.
A field of fallen stones, even one that is carefully labeled and honestly explained to visitors, would teach visitors little about what the fortress once was.
The authenticity of a structure depends partly on how its materials are arranged.
The ministry should not rebuild the east wall unless a record of how its stones were originally laid is found.
Visitors would be unable to tell a rebuilt east wall from one that had never collapsed.
questions.explanation: Okafor says the wall will be rebuilt "from its own original stones," and Lindqvist concedes that "the stones are original," so both are committed to (A). (B) is the near-miss: Lindqvist grants only that a bare field of rubble teaches little. He prefers a well-labeled one, so he isn't committed to saying that it, too, teaches little.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Okafor: Rebuild the wall; rubble teaches nothing, and a wall of original stones is authentic enough.; Lindqvist: The stones are original and bare rubble teaches little, but authenticity also depends on arrangement, which is unknown; a well-labeled ruin is better than a conjecture.

breakdown.analysis: Agreement questions are won in the concessions. Lindqvist opens with two: the stones are original, and a bare field of rubble teaches little. Each candidate agreement must be something Okafor also says. Okafor says both, more or less. But read the answer wording against Lindqvist's exact words: he said "bare" rubble, and he goes on to recommend labeled rubble. An answer that extends his concession to labeled rubble goes beyond what he's committed to. The disagreement proper (whether original materials make the wall authentic) supplies the traps that only one speaker holds.

choices.note: CORRECT. Okafor: rebuilt "from its own original stones." Lindqvist: "The stones are original, I grant you." Both are committed.

The near-miss, failing on "even one that is carefully labeled and honestly explained." Lindqvist concedes only that a bare field teaches little, and he recommends a labeled, "honestly explained" one instead.
Lindqvist's position. Okafor implies that original materials are enough for authenticity, so he isn't committed to this and probably rejects it.
Okafor rejects this. Lindqvist objects to rebuilding without a record, but he never says that finding one would make rebuilding acceptable.
Neither speaker says this. Lindqvist's worry is that a conjecture would be presented as fact, not that it would look seamless.

questions.stimulus: Zoning official: Under the revised code, a building in the historic district can be granted a height variance only if its original facade will be preserved or it is designated as affordable housing. No building that receives public renovation funds can be designated as affordable housing unless at least a quarter of its units are rent-restricted. The Garland Building receives public renovation funds, and only a fifth of its units are rent-restricted. Its owner has nonetheless applied for a variance, pointing out that the Garland's ornate facade is the finest on the block and that she is fully prepared to preserve it. But the facade is in such poor repair that it can be preserved only if the city contributes to the cost of restoring it, and the owner has no means of raising the full cost herself. Hence, the Garland Building cannot be granted a height variance.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the zoning official's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The city contributes to the cost of restoring the facade of every building in the historic district that is designated as affordable housing.
The city contributes to the cost of restoring a building's facade only if that building receives public renovation funds.
No building whose facade is preserved with the help of city funds can be designated as affordable housing.
The Garland's owner would not preserve the facade at her own expense even if she were able to do so.
The city contributes to the cost of restoring a building's facade only if that building is designated as affordable housing.
questions.explanation: A variance requires a preserved facade or affordable designation. Affordable designation is ruled out: with public funds, it needs a quarter of units rent-restricted, and the Garland has a fifth. The facade route requires a city contribution. (E) makes a city contribution require affordable designation, so the facade route collapses into the affordable route, which is already blocked. (A) is the reversal: affordable buildings get contributions, but that doesn't stop a non-affordable one from getting one too.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Garland Building cannot be granted a height variance.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Variance → facade preserved or affordable. Public funds + affordable → at least 25% rent-restricted; the Garland has public funds and 20%. Facade preserved → city contributes.

breakdown.analysis: Diagram it. Variance → (Facade or Affordable). Affordable (with public funds) → ≥25%, and the Garland has 20%, so not Affordable. Facade → City contributes. To kill the variance we must kill Facade, so we need City contributes to lead somewhere already blocked. The cleanest bridge is City contributes → Affordable: then Facade → Contributes → Affordable → ≥25%, which is false. Watch for the reversed arrow and for bridges that lead to a term that's already true (public funds).

choices.note: The reversal: Affordable → Contributes. It says nothing about whether a non-affordable building like the Garland can get a contribution, so the facade route stays open.
The near-miss. Contributes → public funds leads to a fact we already have (the Garland receives public funds), so it blocks nothing. The right bridge leads to "affordable," not "public funds."
This gives Facade (with city help) → not Affordable. The Garland could then preserve its facade with city help, remain non-affordable, and still qualify. Not enough.
The official already says the owner can't raise the full cost herself and the facade can be preserved only with city help, so this adds nothing. Whether the city will contribute is left open.

CORRECT. Facade preserved → city contributes → designated affordable → at least a quarter rent-restricted (because of public funds). The Garland has only a fifth, so both routes to a variance are closed.

questions.stimulus: Library trustee: Ten years ago a local collector left the county library three hundred first editions, on the condition that the collection be kept together and on public display. The library now faces a crisis that no one foresaw when the bequest was made: the reading-room roof, discovered last spring to be structurally unsound, must be replaced, or the reading room will close indefinitely, ending the service on which most of our patrons depend. The board has found no other source of funds, and selling forty of the volumes, the number needed to cover the repair, would leave the remaining two hundred sixty together and on display. Some trustees object that any sale betrays the donor. But the donor's own letters show that she made the gift because she wanted the library to thrive, and a library whose reading room is closed is not thriving. The board should therefore sell the forty volumes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the library trustee's reasoning?
choices: When honoring the condition attached to a gift would, because of circumstances the donor did not foresee, defeat the purpose for which the gift was made, the recipient should depart from that condition to the extent needed to serve that purpose.
A recipient may depart from the condition attached to a gift only if the purpose for which the gift was made could not be served in any other way.
An institution should not accept a gift whose conditions might, under some future circumstances, prevent it from serving the people who depend on it.
A donor's purposes in making a gift should be inferred from the donor's own statements rather than from the conditions the donor attached to the gift.
When the condition attached to a gift can be read in more than one way, the recipient should adopt the reading that best serves the people who depend on it.
questions.explanation: The trustee's facts line up with every clause of (A): an unforeseen circumstance (the roof), honoring the condition would defeat the gift's purpose (a closed reading room means the library isn't thriving), and the sale is limited to what the repair requires (forty volumes). (B) is the trap. It sounds as if it applies, but "only if" gives a necessary condition for departing from the gift's terms, which can never establish that the board should depart from them.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a principle that, applied to the trustee's facts, yields: the board should sell forty volumes despite the gift's condition.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The board should sell forty of the volumes.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The roof crisis was unforeseen; without the repair the reading room closes; no other funds exist; forty is the number needed; the donor's aim was a thriving library.

breakdown.analysis: The trustee piles up specific facts: the crisis was unforeseen, there are no other funds, the sale is limited to the amount needed, and the donor's real purpose was a thriving library. A good justifying principle will be a conditional whose trigger these facts satisfy and whose outcome is "depart from the condition (this far)." Check the outcome first: the answer must say the board should or may depart. Then check every clause against the facts. Watch for a necessary-condition principle ("only if") dressed up as a permission.

choices.note: CORRECT. Unforeseen circumstances (the roof) mean honoring the condition would defeat the purpose (a thriving library), so the board should depart, but only as far as needed (forty volumes). Every element matches a fact the trustee gives.

The trap. The trustee's facts satisfy its condition (no other funds), but "only if" states a requirement for departing, not a license to depart. It can tell you when a sale is forbidden, never that one is called for.
About whether to accept gifts. The gift was accepted years ago; this says nothing about what to do now.
This would let the trustee read the donor's purpose from her letters, but it doesn't say anything about departing from the condition to serve that purpose. Half the bridge.
The condition, keep the collection together and on display, isn't ambiguous, and the trustee doesn't reinterpret it. The trustee proposes breaking it in part.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Across the region, populations of the night-flying Corran moth have fallen by half over the past fifteen years. Some blame a widely used insecticide, but the decline has been just as steep in the region's nature reserves, where that insecticide is banned, as on farmland. A likelier culprit is artificial light. Night-flying moths are drawn to bright lamps, where they circle until exhausted instead of feeding or mating, and during these same fifteen years the region replaced nearly all of its sodium streetlights with LED lamps, which emit far more of the short-wavelength light that such insects find irresistible. It is true that the reserves themselves contain no streetlights. But almost every reserve in the region lies within two kilometers of a lit road. So the switch to LED streetlights, rather than the insecticide, is most likely responsible for the Corran moth's decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ecologist's argument?
choices: Day-flying moth species in the region have declined over the past fifteen years by about the same proportion as the Corran moth.
The insecticide is considerably more toxic to moth caterpillars than to adult moths.
Adult Corran moths regularly fly several kilometers in a single night.
In the parts of the region where sodium streetlights have not yet been replaced, Corran moth populations have also fallen by about half.
Corran moths are drawn to sodium streetlights just as strongly as they are drawn to LED lamps.
questions.explanation: The ecologist uses the reserves to rule out the insecticide, but then has to explain how streetlights could hurt moths in reserves that have no streetlights. The answer offered is proximity: reserves are within two kilometers of lit roads. That only matters if reserve moths actually reach those roads, and (C) says they easily can. (E) is the trap: it sounds like more evidence that moths love lamps, but it means the switch to LEDs changed nothing.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The switch to LED streetlights, not the insecticide, is most likely responsible for the moth's decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The decline is as steep in reserves (no insecticide) as on farmland; LEDs attract night-flying insects more; reserves lie within two kilometers of lit roads.

breakdown.analysis: Spot the concession and how it's answered. The reserves have no streetlights, so the ecologist bridges the gap with 'within two kilometers of a lit road'. That bridge holds only if the moths travel that far. Prephrase: Corran moths range at least a couple of kilometers. Also notice the conclusion is about the switch to LEDs specifically, so anything that makes old and new lamps equivalent hurts the argument.

choices.note: If moths that never fly at night have declined just as much, something other than night lighting is likely at work. This weakens.
Caterpillar versus adult toxicity doesn't change the key fact that the insecticide is banned in reserves where moths declined anyway. No effect.

CORRECT. Moths that range several kilometers a night can easily reach lit roads two kilometers from the reserves, which explains how streetlights could cause the decline inside reserves that have none.
If moths fell by half where the old sodium lamps remain, the switch to LEDs can't be what caused the decline. This weakens.

The trap. It sounds like support for the lighting theory, but if moths are just as attracted to sodium lamps, replacing them with LEDs made no difference, and the conclusion credits the switch. This weakens.

questions.stimulus:
Arvid: Cities should not subsidize professional sports stadiums. Study after study finds that a new stadium does not increase a region's total spending on entertainment; it merely shifts spending away from restaurants, theaters, and other local venues. A public investment that only relocates economic activity, rather than adding to it, is a waste of taxpayers' money.

Beatriz: By that standard you would have to oppose the new central library you campaigned for last year. Its supporters, you among them, never claimed it would raise the region's total spending on anything; they argued that it would give residents something of value they could not get otherwise. If benefits of that kind can justify public spending on a library, then the question to ask about a stadium is not whether it adds to total spending, but whether it gives residents something of value they could not get otherwise. On that question, your studies say nothing.
questions.stem: Beatriz responds to Arvid by
choices: calling into question the reliability of the studies on which Arvid's argument relies
arguing that Arvid's past conduct gives reason to doubt his sincerity in advancing the standard he proposes
maintaining that a stadium and a library differ in ways that Arvid's argument fails to take into account
showing that the standard Arvid invokes would, if applied consistently, count against something he endorses, and proposing a different standard that his evidence does not address
showing that the standard Arvid invokes would, if applied consistently, count against something he endorses, and concluding that cities should therefore be willing to subsidize stadiums after all
questions.explanation: Beatriz turns Arvid's standard (spending that only relocates activity is wasted) on the library he backed, which also added no total spending. She then names a better test, whether residents get something of value they couldn't otherwise get, and points out that his studies don't speak to it: (D). (E) shares the first half but adds a conclusion she never draws. She says only that the studies are silent on the right question.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Beatriz: whether total spending rises is the wrong test for a stadium; the right test is one Arvid's evidence doesn't address.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Arvid's standard would condemn the library he supported, which was justified by giving residents something of value, not by raising total spending.

breakdown.analysis: Describe Beatriz's moves before you look at the choices. Move 1: apply Arvid's principle to a case he accepts and show that it gives the wrong answer there. Move 2: offer the standard that actually justified that case and note that his studies are silent on it. Notice what she does NOT do: she doesn't dispute the studies, doesn't say the stadium should be funded, and doesn't question his motives. In abstract method answers, every clause has to be true.

choices.note: Beatriz accepts the studies' finding and says only that they answer the wrong question.
She points to his library campaign to test his principle, not to question his sincerity. The inconsistency is used against the standard, not against the person.
The opposite. Her argument works only because she treats the library and the stadium as relevantly alike, judged by the same test.
CORRECT. Arvid's standard would condemn the library he endorses (move 1), and she substitutes the value-to-residents test, about which his studies "say nothing" (move 2).
The near-miss. The first clause is right, but Beatriz never concludes that stadiums should be subsidized. She leaves that question open under the new test.

questions.stimulus: Foundation policy: A research proposal can be funded only if it has been reviewed by the full grants committee, and no proposal is reviewed by the full committee unless an external referee has evaluated it. External referees evaluate a proposal only if its budget is under the foundation's cap or the director has granted it a budget waiver. The director grants waivers only to proposals that include a data-sharing plan, and every proposal that includes a data-sharing plan is posted in the foundation's public registry. Proposals submitted through the confidential track are never posted in the public registry. Finally, any proposal whose budget is under the cap is automatically eligible for the foundation's expedited review, although being eligible for expedited review does not by itself guarantee that a proposal will be reviewed by the full committee or funded.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Any proposal that includes a data-sharing plan but whose budget is not under the cap will be evaluated by an external referee.
Every proposal that the foundation funds is posted in its public registry.
No proposal submitted through the confidential track is evaluated by an external referee.
No proposal submitted through the confidential track is funded unless its budget is under the foundation's cap.
Every proposal that is eligible for expedited review and has been evaluated by an external referee is reviewed by the full committee.
questions.explanation: The chain: funded → full-committee review → external referee → (under cap or waiver). And waiver → data-sharing plan → public registry → not confidential track. So a confidential-track proposal can't have a waiver, and if it's funded it must be under the cap. That's (D). (B) is the trap: it forgets the under-the-cap route, which leads to funding without any registry posting.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: Funded → full-committee review → external referee → (under cap OR waiver). Waiver → data-sharing plan → public registry. Confidential track → NOT public registry. Under cap → eligible for expedited review (which guarantees nothing).

breakdown.analysis: Draw the chain and its contrapositives. Confidential → not posted → no data-sharing plan → no waiver. A funded proposal had a referee, so it was under the cap or had a waiver; with the waiver ruled out, it must be under the cap. Watch the 'or' split: answers that forget the under-cap branch are too strong, and answers that run an arrow backward are reversals. The expedited-review sentence is a dead end.

choices.note: Reverses the arrows. A waiver is required for referee evaluation of an over-cap proposal, but a data-sharing plan doesn't guarantee a waiver, and a waiver doesn't guarantee evaluation.
The near-miss. A funded proposal could have been under the cap with no waiver, no data-sharing plan, and no registry posting. True only of funded proposals not under the cap.
Too strong. A confidential proposal can't get a waiver, but if its budget is under the cap, a referee may still evaluate it.
CORRECT. Confidential → not posted → no data-sharing plan → no waiver. Funded → referee → under cap or waiver. With no waiver, a funded confidential proposal must be under the cap.

Reverses 'no full-committee review unless a referee has evaluated it'. A referee's evaluation is required for committee review, not a guarantee of it, and the expedited-review eligibility guarantees nothing.

questions.stimulus: Gardener: The Ellery rose will thrive in our new north bed. Because that bed's soil is dense clay and it falls into shade soon after midday, any rose variety that tolerates heavy clay will thrive there unless the variety needs full sun. The Ellery rose certainly tolerates heavy clay: it has been grown for generations in the clay-soil gardens of the river valley, where most other roses struggle. Some visitors have warned us that the Ellery rose is a sun lover, and it is true that it flowers most abundantly when it receives full sun all day. But flowering most abundantly in full sun is not the same as needing full sun, and experienced growers agree that the Ellery rose flowers well even in partial shade, just as it does in the half-shaded courtyard beds of the old abbey garden a few miles from here.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the gardener's argument?
choices: Ravi's essay will be included in the anthology, since the editors include every essay that is submitted before the deadline unless it exceeds the length limit. Although Ravi's essay is longer than any essay the editors have accepted in the past, the limit was raised this year, and his essay does not exceed it.

Every hand-stitched quilt entered at the fair will receive a ribbon unless it exceeds the size limit, so Mara's quilt will receive a ribbon. Her quilt is hand-stitched, as the judges confirmed by examining its seams. It is larger than any quilt that has won before, but being larger than past winners is not the same as exceeding the limit, and her quilt is within it.

Every vehicle that passes inspection may use the old bridge unless it is over the weight limit. Tomas's truck passed inspection last month. Although his truck is heavier than most of the vehicles that use the bridge, no one has shown that it is over the weight limit, so his truck may use the bridge.

Any applicant with a law degree will be hired by the firm unless she lacks trial experience. Lena has a law degree. She has observed many trials, but observing trials is not the same as having trial experience, and she has never taken part in one. So Lena will not be hired by the firm.

Most dogs that are calm around children will do well in a family home unless they need a large yard. Rufus is calm around children, and although he enjoys running in large yards, enjoying a large yard is not the same as needing one. So Rufus will probably do well in a family home.
questions.explanation: The gardener's pattern: every A is C unless it is B; x is A (with support); x has a feature that resembles B but is not B; so x is C. (B) matches every step, with the conclusion moved to the front. (E) is the near-miss: it copies the wording, including 'is not the same as', but its rule is about 'most' dogs and its conclusion is only probable.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the pattern: every A is C unless it is B. x is A (supported). x has B', which looks like B but isn't B. So x is C.

breakdown.analysis: Strip the content. Rule: all clay-tolerant roses thrive unless they need full sun. Fact: Ellery is clay-tolerant (with evidence). Rebutted objection: it loves full sun, but loving isn't needing, and it doesn't need it. Conclusion: it will thrive. Check each choice for (1) a universal rule with an 'unless' exception, (2) proof that x meets the condition, (3) a positive showing, not just an absence of evidence, that the exception doesn't apply, and (4) a positive conclusion. The conclusion's position doesn't matter.

choices.note: Never establishes that Ravi's essay was submitted before the deadline, so it skips the step that shows x meets the rule's condition. The gardener proves the Ellery rose tolerates clay.

CORRECT. Universal rule with an exception (hand-stitched quilts get ribbons unless oversized), the condition met with support (judges checked the seams), a look-alike to the exception rebutted (larger than past winners isn't over the limit), positive conclusion. Only the order differs.
Rules out the exception only because no one has shown it applies, an appeal to absence of evidence. The gardener shows positively that the rose doesn't need full sun.

Uses the same 'is not the same as' step, but to find that the exception does apply and then concludes Lena won't be hired. The rule never says what happens when the exception applies. Different, and invalid.
The near-miss. Almost word for word, but 'most dogs' and 'probably' turn a certain rule into a probable one. The gardener's rule covers every clay-tolerant rose.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: When an employee asks to work from home, the employer should approve the request if every one of the employee's duties can be performed remotely and the employee received at least a satisfactory rating in his or her most recent performance review, unless approving the request would leave the employee's team with no one physically present at some time when the law requires on-site staff. The first two conditions protect the employer's legitimate interest in having the work done well; the exception reflects the fact that legal obligations take precedence over individual preferences. It should be stressed, however, that this principle says only when a request must be approved. Nothing in it implies that an employer must refuse a request that falls outside it, and employers remain free to be more generous than it demands.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: All of Dara's duties can be performed remotely, and her most recent review rated her excellent. Her manager nonetheless turned down her request because two of her teammates already work from home. The manager therefore acted wrongly.
All of Felix's duties can be performed remotely, but his most recent performance review was unsatisfactory. So his employer should deny his request to work from home.

Gita's most recent review was satisfactory, and her teammates cover every period when the law requires on-site staff. One of her duties, signing for deliveries, can be done only on site, but it takes up very little of her time. So her employer should approve her request.

All of Hal's duties can be performed remotely and his most recent review was satisfactory, but approving his request would leave his team with no one on site during hours when the law requires on-site staff. So his employer should deny the request.

Inez's most recent performance review rated her satisfactory, though her earlier reviews were poor, and all of her duties can be performed remotely. Several of her teammates are on site throughout every period in which the law requires on-site staff, and none of them has asked to work from home. So her employer should approve her request.
questions.explanation: The principle requires approval when (1) every duty can be done remotely, (2) the most recent review was at least satisfactory, and (3) the exception doesn't apply. It never requires refusal. Only (E) establishes all three and concludes 'approve'. (C) is the near-miss: one on-site duty, however small, fails 'every one of the employee's duties'.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Principle: approve IF every duty can be done remotely AND the most recent review was at least satisfactory, UNLESS approval would leave no one on site when the law requires it. The principle never requires refusal.

breakdown.analysis: Write the principle as: (all duties remote) AND (latest review satisfactory) AND NOT (exception) → must approve. Then sort the choices. Any choice concluding 'deny' or 'should refuse' can't conform, since the ethicist says outright that the principle never requires refusal. A choice concluding 'approve' (or 'acted wrongly' in refusing) must establish all three elements; look for one that quietly fails a condition or leaves the exception unsettled.

choices.note: The exception is left open. Two teammates working from home doesn't tell us whether Dara's leaving would empty the office when the law requires staff, so the principle doesn't establish that refusing her was wrong.
Failing a condition means the principle doesn't require approval, but the ethicist says it never requires refusal. 'Should deny' doesn't follow.
The near-miss. The principle requires that every duty be doable remotely. Signing for deliveries can't be, however small a part of her job it is, so the principle doesn't require approval.
The exception applies, so the principle simply doesn't require approval. It doesn't say to deny, and the ethicist stresses that.

CORRECT. All duties are remote; the most recent review (the one that counts) is satisfactory; teammates cover every period the law requires, and none plans to leave, so the exception doesn't apply. The principle requires approval.

questions.stimulus: Labor economist: Several commentators have claimed that the recent four-day-workweek trials, in which participating firms reported steady or rising output after cutting a day from the week, prove that shorter workweeks would raise productivity throughout the economy. That claim does not survive scrutiny. The firms that volunteered for the trials were overwhelmingly ones whose work is judged by its output rather than by hours on the job, such as software developers, design studios, and consultancies. Such firms can compress five days of work into four far more readily than hospitals, factories, or shops can, since what those businesses produce depends on someone being present during fixed hours. The trials therefore reveal little about how a shorter week would fare in the sectors that employ most workers. This is not to dismiss the trials: they show convincingly that, for work judged by its output, giving up a day need not mean giving up output. But a result from a self-selected group of firms cannot simply be stretched to cover the whole economy.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion drawn in the labor economist's argument?
choices: The four-day-workweek trials reveal little about how a shorter week would fare in the sectors that employ most workers.
