For work that is judged by its output, a four-day workweek need not reduce output.
The four-day-workweek trials do not establish that a shorter workweek would raise productivity across the economy as a whole.
A shorter workweek would lower productivity in hospitals, factories, and shops.
The results of the four-day-workweek trials do not show that a shorter workweek raises productivity in any sector of the economy.
questions.explanation: The economist states a view (the trials prove economy-wide productivity gains) and rejects it: 'That claim does not survive scrutiny.' Everything else supports that rejection, including the intermediate conclusion that the trials say little about most sectors (A). (C) restates the rejection. (E) is the near-miss: by saying 'in any sector', it goes further than the economist, who denies only the economy-wide claim.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The commentators' claim, that the trials prove shorter workweeks would raise productivity throughout the economy, is unwarranted.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The volunteer firms were mostly output-judged firms, which can compress work more easily than hours-bound sectors; so (sub-conclusion) the trials say little about most sectors. Concession: the trials do show output-judged work needn't lose output.

breakdown.analysis: When an argument opens with someone else's view, the main conclusion is usually the author's verdict on it, here the flat 'That claim does not survive scrutiny.' Fill in the pronoun: the claim that the trials prove economy-wide gains. The 'therefore' sentence is an intermediate conclusion that supports the verdict, and the 'This is not to dismiss' sentence is a concession. Match the scope exactly: the economist denies an economy-wide claim, not every claim.

choices.note: The sub-conclusion. It's marked by 'therefore' and is drawn from the facts about the volunteer firms, but it serves to support the rejection of the commentators' claim.
The concession. The economist grants this to show that the trials aren't worthless; it isn't the point being argued.

CORRECT. This paraphrases 'That claim does not survive scrutiny': the trials don't prove shorter weeks would raise productivity throughout the economy. Everything else in the argument is offered to support it.
Too strong. The economist says the trials reveal little about those sectors, not that shorter weeks would hurt them.
The near-miss. 'In any sector' goes too far. The economist rejects only the economy-wide claim and never says the trials show nothing about any sector.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Halloran's letters show that in the spring of 1784 he twice traveled the old post road between the coast and the capital, a road that passes within a day's ride of the monastery at Cressing. The monastery's guest register for that spring, which survives intact, records a single overnight guest described only as "a trader from the coast." Some scholars dismiss the identification of this guest with Halloran, noting that dozens of coastal traders used the same road each season. But their objection proves very little. At most it establishes that the guest might have been someone other than Halloran; it does nothing to show that he was. Every piece of evidence we possess, by contrast, is consistent with Halloran's having stopped at Cressing, and none of it tells against that. We can therefore conclude that the guest recorded in the register was Halloran.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the historian's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: fails to consider that the monastery's guest register might have omitted some of the people who stayed there that spring
presumes, without providing justification, that Halloran's route between the coast and the capital took him near the monastery
faults an objection for showing only that an alternative is possible, while resting its own conclusion on evidence that the scholars who raised the objection themselves accept as accurate
faults an objection for showing only that an alternative is possible, while resting its own conclusion on considerations that show no more than that its own view is possible
treats a fact that, if anything, casts doubt on the identification as though it provided support for that identification
questions.explanation: The historian dismisses the scholars because their point shows only that the guest might have been someone else, then concludes the guest was Halloran from the fact that the evidence is consistent with it, which shows only that he might have been. That double standard, a possibility treated as proof, is (D). (C) copies the first half but ends with a description that isn't a flaw: relying on evidence both sides accept is perfectly proper.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The guest recorded as "a trader from the coast" was Halloran.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Halloran used a road near the monastery twice that spring; the register lists one unnamed coastal trader; the scholars' objection shows only that it might have been someone else; all the evidence is consistent with its being Halloran.

breakdown.analysis: Hold the historian to his own standard. He says the objection fails because it shows only a possibility. But what is his own case? "Every piece of evidence is consistent with" Halloran's visit and "none tells against it": that also shows only a possibility. With dozens of traders on the road, consistency is cheap. So the flaw is possibility-to-certainty, sharpened by applying a demanding standard to the opponents and a lax one to himself. (C) and (D) share their opening; read their endings word by word.

choices.note: If the register omitted some guests, that wouldn't undermine the identification at all; the recorded guest is still a coastal trader who might be Halloran. Not a weakness of the argument.
The letters establish this: the road he traveled passes within a day's ride of Cressing. Nothing is presumed.

The near-miss. The first half is exactly right, but the second half names no error. Both sides accept the letters and the register, and drawing a conclusion from shared evidence is fine. The problem is that the evidence shows only possibility.
CORRECT. The objection is dismissed for establishing only a possibility, and the conclusion rests on mere consistency, which also establishes only a possibility. Possibility is treated as certainty.
The historian never treats the dozens of traders as support. He dismisses that fact as proving little; he doesn't recruit it to his side.

questions.stimulus: Conservator: Some argue that the faded frescoes in the chapel should be repainted so as to restore the colors the artist intended. But we cannot know what colors the artist intended. Chemical analysis shows that the pigments he used have darkened and shifted in hue, unevenly, over five centuries, so their present appearance is no reliable guide to their original one; and no written description of the frescoes from his lifetime survives. Without such knowledge, any repainting would substitute a modern restorer's guesses for the artist's work, while covering the only physical evidence of that work that remains. Thus, whatever its intentions, repainting would bring the frescoes no closer to the artist's vision and would make them less his own. The chapel's trustees should therefore limit themselves to stabilizing the existing paint.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the conservator's argument by the claim that we cannot know what colors the artist intended?
choices: It is a claim advanced by those whose position the conservator opposes, and the argument aims to show that it is mistaken.
It is the main conclusion of the argument, which the conservator's other statements are offered to support.
It is supported by other statements in the argument and is used to support a claim that is in turn offered in support of the argument's main conclusion.
It is a premise offered without support, which the argument uses to establish that the present appearance of the pigments is an unreliable guide.
It is supported by other statements in the argument and is offered as the sole basis for the claim that repainting would cover the only physical evidence of the artist's work.
questions.explanation: The claim is backed by the pigment analysis and the missing descriptions. It then supports the claim that repainting would substitute guesses for the artist's work, which supports "no closer to his vision," which in turn supports the main conclusion that the trustees should only stabilize the paint: (C). (D) runs the support backwards, and (E) attaches the claim to the one part of that sentence that doesn't depend on it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The trustees should limit themselves to stabilizing the existing paint.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pigment changes and the lack of contemporary descriptions → we cannot know the intended colors → repainting would substitute guesses and cover the original → repainting brings the frescoes no closer to the artist's vision → only stabilize.

breakdown.analysis: Build the chain. The claim follows "But," which marks the conservator's reply to the repainters. The next sentence supports it (the pigments shifted; no descriptions survive). The sentence after begins "Without such knowledge", so it depends on the claim. "Thus" draws a further conclusion, and "therefore" draws the final one. So the claim is an early intermediate conclusion, two steps from the end. Watch for answers that give it the wrong neighbor.

choices.note: The opponents claim they can restore the intended colors. "We cannot know" is the conservator's own claim, made against them.
The main conclusion is the final "therefore" sentence, about what the trustees should do. This claim sits several steps earlier.

CORRECT. It receives support (pigment analysis, no descriptions) and supports "repainting would substitute guesses," which in turn supports, through the "Thus" claim, the conclusion about stabilizing.
Backwards. The pigments' unreliability is evidence FOR the claim, not something the claim establishes, and the claim is not unsupported.

The near-miss. The first half is right, but the claim supports the "substitute guesses" part of that sentence. That repainting covers the only physical evidence follows from repainting itself, not from our ignorance of the intended colors.

questions.stimulus:
Critic: The regional arts council has become far too cautious. Most of its grant money now goes to long-established institutions, and it rarely funds experimental work.

Council director: The critic's charge does not survive scrutiny. The council does not make grant decisions as a single body; it acts through five independent review panels, one each for visual art, music, theater, dance, and literature. And the record of each panel tells against the charge. Every one of the five has, in each of the last three years, awarded at least one grant to an artist who had never before received public funding, and several of those awards went to work that reviewers later described as boldly experimental. A panel that repeatedly takes chances on untested artists cannot fairly be called cautious. Since none of the council's panels is cautious, the council itself is not cautious either.
questions.stem: The council director's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: attempts to discredit the critic's charge by questioning whether the critic understands how the council's five independent panels actually reach their grant decisions
takes for granted that a group as a whole cannot have a characteristic unless each of its components has that characteristic
relies on the assessments of reviewers without establishing that those reviewers are qualified to judge experimental work
fails to consider that funding artists who have never before received public money is not the only way a panel might take risks
takes for granted that a group as a whole cannot have a characteristic unless at least one of its components has that characteristic
questions.explanation: The director infers that the council is not cautious because no panel is. That presumes the whole could be cautious only if some part were. But five panels that each make one daring grant a year can add up to a council whose money mostly goes to established institutions, which is exactly the critic's charge. (B) differs from the key by a single word: "each" instead of "at least one," which is not what the director's inference requires.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The council is not cautious.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The council acts through five panels; each panel has funded at least one first-time artist every year, so no panel is cautious; therefore the council isn't.

breakdown.analysis: Map the final inference. "None of the panels is cautious, so the council isn't." Contrapositive: if the council is cautious, at least one panel is. That's the part-whole assumption. And it fails here: each panel clears the director's low bar (one daring grant a year) while the council's money, taken together, still goes mostly to established institutions. Then pin down the exact quantifier. The director needs "cautious whole → some cautious part," not "→ every part cautious."

choices.note: The director describes the panel structure but never questions the critic's knowledge or standing. No attack on the source.

The near-miss. Saying the whole is cautious only if every panel is would make the director's inference weaker, not stronger: one non-cautious panel would then be enough. The director's step needs only "at least one". This choice fails on the word "each."
The reviewers' praise is a side point ("several of those awards"). The core evidence is first-time grants, so the argument doesn't depend on the reviewers' qualifications.
Other ways of taking risks would only add to the director's case. Overlooking them is no flaw in an argument that the council isn't cautious.

CORRECT. "None of the panels is cautious, so the council isn't" assumes the council could be cautious only if some panel were. A whole can have a property, mostly funding the safe choice, that none of its parts shows by the director's measure.

questions.stimulus: Editor: We should not run the investigative piece on the Brennick factory in its current form. Our policy is to publish an accusation of wrongdoing only if it is supported either by documents we have independently verified or by at least two named sources. The piece's central accusation, that the factory falsified its safety inspection reports, rests on three sources, but only one of them has agreed to be named. The reporter also obtained an internal memo, and that memo has been authenticated by the reporter's contact inside the company, but not by us. The reporter protests that the two unnamed sources have been reliable in the past and that the memo is almost certainly genuine. Both claims may well be true. But our policy is about naming and verification, not about likely reliability, and as the piece now stands it does not satisfy that policy.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the editor's argument?
choices: The internal memo obtained by the reporter is not genuine.
The two unnamed sources would refuse to be named if the reporter asked them again.
The magazine has not independently verified any document, other than the memo, that supports the piece's central accusation.
Sources who refuse to be named are, in general, less reliable than sources who agree to be named.
Every accusation the piece makes, other than its central one, satisfies the magazine's policy on naming sources and verifying documents.
questions.explanation: The policy is a disjunction: verified documents OR two named sources. The editor knocks out the named-sources route (only one) and the memo, but the piece could still qualify through some other document the magazine has verified. The argument needs there to be none, (C). (B) is the near-miss: it would matter for a revised piece, but the conclusion is limited to the piece "in its current form."

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Brennick piece should not run in its current form.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: An accusation may run only if backed by documents the magazine verified or by two named sources; the central accusation has one named source, and the memo was verified only by the reporter's contact.

breakdown.analysis: "Only if A or B": to show an accusation can't run, the editor must show both A and B fail. B (two named sources) clearly fails. For A, the editor rules out one document, the memo. But A is about documents in general. Any other verified document would satisfy the policy. That's the gap. Note the concessions (the sources are reliable, the memo is probably genuine). The editor sets them aside as irrelevant to the policy, so no answer about reliability or authenticity can be required.

choices.note: The editor concedes the memo may well be genuine; the problem is who verified it.
choices.negation: The memo is genuine. The editor already allows this; it still isn't verified by the magazine. Survives.

choices.note: The near-miss. Whether the sources might be named later matters only for a future version. The conclusion concerns the piece "in its current form," where only one is named.
choices.negation: The unnamed sources would agree to be named if asked. The piece as it stands still names only one. Survives.

choices.note: CORRECT. The policy can be met by verified documents. The editor eliminates only the memo, so the argument requires that no other verified document backs the accusation.
choices.negation: The magazine HAS verified some other document supporting the central accusation. Then the accusation meets the policy, and the argument collapses.

choices.note: The editor explicitly says the policy is about naming, not reliability, so no claim about reliability is needed.
choices.negation: Unnamed sources are as reliable as named ones. Irrelevant under a naming rule. Survives.

choices.note: If some other accusation also failed, that would only add to the case against running the piece. Not required.
choices.negation: Some other accusation in the piece also fails the standard. That's another reason not to run it. Survives.

questions.stimulus: Wellness researcher: A recent study surveyed members of the online community attached to a popular meditation app. Of the 1,800 members who had meditated with the app daily for at least two years, 81 percent reported substantially lower stress than when they began, compared with only 37 percent of members who had meditated daily for less than six months. These differences persisted after the researchers controlled for members' age, income, and exercise habits, and blood tests on a subsample confirmed lower levels of a stress hormone among the long-term meditators, so the reports cannot be dismissed as wishful thinking. Critics object that the community's members are self-selected, but every member joined within a month of first downloading the app, so the long-term and short-term groups were recruited in exactly the same way. Thus, most people who take up daily meditation can expect a substantial reduction in their stress if they keep it up for two years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the wellness researcher's argument?
choices: Members of the app's online community exercise more often, on average, than do adults of the same age in the general population as a whole.
Most people who begin meditating daily with the app give it up within a year, typically because they notice no change in their stress.
Some members who had meditated daily for at least two years reported that their stress was higher than when they began.
Members who had meditated daily for less than six months were, on average, younger than the long-term meditators.
People who meditate daily without using any app report reduced stress about as often as app users do.
questions.explanation: The researcher answers the worry about recruitment, but not the worry about who stays. If most beginners quit within a year because meditation isn't helping them, the two-year group is a filtered set of people it already worked for, and the 81 percent says little about what would happen to a typical beginner who kept going. That is (B). (D) is the trap: age was already controlled for.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most people who take up daily meditation can expect substantially lower stress if they keep it up for two years.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 81 percent of two-year users vs. 37 percent of under-six-month users report lower stress; confounds (age, income, exercise) controlled; blood tests back the reports; both groups were recruited the same way.

breakdown.analysis: The researcher closes three doors: confounds, wishful thinking, and recruitment bias. The open door is attrition. The two-year group isn't a random sample of beginners who persisted; it's whoever chose to persist, and people tend to persist with what works for them. So prephrase: the people who reached two years differ from typical beginners because the non-responders dropped out. Ignore any answer that re-raises a factor the stimulus already controlled for.

choices.note: Comparing members with the general population is beside the point, and exercise habits were controlled for within the study. No effect on the argument.

CORRECT. If most beginners quit because they feel no benefit, the long-term group is made up largely of people for whom meditation already worked. Their 81 percent can't be projected onto 'most people who take up daily meditation', many of whom are the non-responders who quit.

The near-miss. 'Some' long-term users reporting more stress is already allowed by the 81 percent figure (19 percent didn't improve). It tells us nothing new and doesn't touch the conclusion about most people.
Tempting because it names a difference between the groups, but the researchers controlled for age. A controlled-for difference can't explain away the result.
Whether app-free meditators do as well is irrelevant: the conclusion is about daily meditation, not about the app. If anything, this fits the claim that meditation helps.

questions.stimulus: Health analyst: Last year, Dunmore's two public hospitals, Northgate and Riverside, together performed 2,000 knee replacements, 1,500 of them at Northgate. Within a year of surgery, 3 percent of Northgate's knee-replacement patients needed a second operation on the same knee, compared with 5 percent of Riverside's. Riverside's administrators argue that this comparison is unfair: under city policy, every knee replacement on a patient over the age of seventy-five is performed at Northgate, and such patients accounted for 40 percent of Northgate's knee replacements last year. But Northgate's record holds up even when those patients are set aside. Among its knee-replacement patients aged seventy-five or younger, only 2 percent needed a second operation within a year, a figure well below Riverside's rate for patients who, under the city's policy, all fall in that same age group.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following is most strongly supported by them?
choices: Most of the knee replacements performed in Dunmore last year that were followed by a second operation within a year had been performed on patients over seventy-five.
Had Riverside performed the knee replacements on patients over seventy-five, its overall rate of second operations would have exceeded 5 percent.
Riverside performed more knee replacements on patients aged seventy-five or younger than Northgate did.
Among Northgate's patients, the rate of second operations for those over seventy-five was more than twice the hospital's overall rate.
Northgate's knee-replacement patients over seventy-five needed a second operation at a lower rate than Riverside's knee-replacement patients did.
questions.explanation: Work out the numbers: Northgate had 600 patients over seventy-five and 900 aged seventy-five or younger. Its 45 second operations (3 percent of 1,500) include 18 among the younger group (2 percent of 900), so 27 were among the older group: 27 of 600 is 4.5 percent, which is below Riverside's 5 percent. That's (E). (A) is the trap: 27 of the city's 70 second operations is well under half.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 2,000 knee replacements: 1,500 at Northgate (3 percent second operations), 500 at Riverside (5 percent). All patients over 75 go to Northgate, making up 40 percent of its cases. Northgate's 75-and-under rate is 2 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Build the table before reading the choices. Northgate: 600 over 75, 900 aged 75 or younger. Second operations: 45 total, 18 among the younger, so 27 among the older (4.5 percent). Riverside: 500 patients, all 75 or younger, 25 second operations. City total: 70. Then test each choice against the table. Intuition says older patients do worse than everyone, but the numbers don't bear that out against Riverside.

choices.note: Second operations among patients over seventy-five: 27. City total: 45 + 25 = 70. 27 is not most of 70. The tempting arithmetic trap.
We know nothing about how Riverside would do with older patients. This is speculation the data can't support.
Northgate performed 900 operations on patients aged seventy-five or younger; Riverside performed 500. The reverse is true.
The older patients' rate is 4.5 percent; Northgate's overall rate is 3 percent. 4.5 is one and a half times 3, not more than twice.
CORRECT. Northgate's 45 second operations minus the 18 among its 900 younger patients leaves 27 among its 600 older patients: 4.5 percent, which is below Riverside's 5 percent.

questions.stimulus: Lab director: Priya Rao designed the sampling protocol our team used to gather the river-sediment data for our forthcoming paper, but she left the lab before any samples were collected and has had no part in analyzing the data or drafting the paper. Several team members argue that she should be listed as a coauthor because the study could not have been carried out without a sampling protocol. That reason proves too much: the study also could not have been carried out without the technicians who maintained our equipment, and no one proposes listing them. Still, Rao's protocol was not a routine adaptation of an existing method. It introduced a new way of selecting sampling sites, and that innovation is precisely what allows our findings to address questions that earlier studies could not. Rao should therefore be listed as a coauthor.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the lab director's reasoning?
choices: Anyone who made an original contribution on which a study's distinctive findings depend should be listed as a coauthor, whether or not that person helped collect or analyze the data.
Anyone who designs the method a study uses should be listed as a coauthor, provided that he or she was a member of the research team when the data were collected.
Anyone whose contribution to a study consisted of routinely adapting an existing method should be thanked in the acknowledgments rather than listed as a coauthor.
Someone who took no part in analyzing a study's data or drafting its report should be listed as a coauthor only if his or her contribution was original.
The contributions of those who maintain a study's equipment deserve recognition as substantial as that given to the contributions of those who design its methods.
questions.explanation: The director rejects 'the study needed it' as a reason and rests the case on originality: Rao's new site-selection method is what makes the findings distinctive. (A) turns that into a sufficient condition for coauthorship regardless of her absence from collection and analysis. (D) is the trap: it makes originality NECESSARY for an absent contributor's coauthorship, which never establishes that Rao should be listed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the principle that makes 'Rao should be a coauthor' follow from the director's reasons.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Rao should be listed as a coauthor.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Her protocol was original (a new site-selection method) and is what lets the findings answer new questions; (rebuttal) mere necessity proves too much, since the technicians were necessary too.

breakdown.analysis: The director gives one reason and rejects another. The justifying principle must use the accepted reason (an original contribution the findings depend on) as a SUFFICIENT condition for coauthorship, and must not be defeated by Rao's absence from data collection and analysis. Check provisos against the facts and watch for 'only if'.

choices.note: CORRECT. Rao's site-selection method is original and is what the findings depend on, and the principle explicitly sets aside her absence from data collection and analysis. Coauthorship follows.
Near miss. Rao designed the method, but she left before any data were collected, so the proviso fails and the principle doesn't apply to her.
This addresses routine adaptations, and Rao's protocol wasn't one. The principle is silent about her.
The 'only if' makes originality a necessary condition. Rao meets it, but meeting a necessary condition doesn't establish that she should be listed.
This is about technicians and, if anything, cuts against the director's distinction between them and Rao. It says nothing about who should be a coauthor.

questions.stimulus: Literary columnist: Most of the novels shortlisted for this year's Harwick Prize were released by small independent presses, a fact the judges have repeatedly cited, in interviews, in their published remarks, and at the announcement ceremony itself, as proof that the prize rewards literary merit rather than marketing muscle. But consider carefully what that boast implies about the shortlisted books themselves. Most of the books that small independent presses released this year received no promotion whatsoever: no advertising, no author tours, not even review copies sent to national newspapers. And any book that receives no promotion depends entirely on word of mouth for whatever readers it manages to find. So, whatever the judges may intend, at least one of the novels on this year's shortlist must depend entirely on word of mouth for its readers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the literary columnist's argument?
choices: Most of the paintings now hanging in the museum's east gallery are by Ruiz. Every painting by Ruiz in the museum is on loan from a private collector, and every painting on loan from a private collector must be returned to its owner by the first day of spring. So at least one painting in the east gallery must be returned to its owner by the first day of spring.

Every member of the city orchestra is a trained sight-reader. Most of the musicians who auditioned this week are trained sight-readers, and most trained sight-readers in the city have played in a professional ensemble. So most of the musicians who auditioned this week must be members of the city orchestra.

Anyone who has volunteered at the Fernhill shelter has received first-aid training. Most of the students in Dr. Osei's seminar belong to the campus outdoors club, and most members of the outdoors club have volunteered at the Fernhill shelter. So at least one student in Dr. Osei's seminar must have received first-aid training.

Most residents of Larch Street own a car, and most residents of Larch Street have signed the petition for a new bus line. Anyone who has signed the petition will be invited to the transit meeting. So at least one car owner on Larch Street must be invited to the transit meeting.

Most of the trails in Harlow Park are open to cyclists, and most trails open to cyclists are paved. Any paved trail must be inspected monthly. So at least one trail in Harlow Park that is not open to cyclists must be inspected monthly.
questions.explanation: The columnist chains two "most" statements about different groups: most shortlisted novels are small-press books, and most small-press books got no promotion. Since small-press books far outnumber the shortlist, the shortlisted ones could all be among the promoted minority. (C) has the same structure with its premises reordered: all volunteers have training; most seminar students are in the club; most club members volunteered. (D) looks the same but is valid, because its two "most" statements are about the same group, so they must overlap.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the flaw: Most A are B; most B are C; all C are D; so at least one A is D. The two "most" statements cover different groups, so the A's may fall entirely outside the C's.

breakdown.analysis: Abstract the stimulus: shortlisted (A) → mostly small-press (B); small-press books (B) → mostly unpromoted (C); unpromoted (C) → all word-of-mouth (D); conclusion: some A is D. The invalid link is most-of-A-in-B plus most-of-B-in-C. B is a big group, and A can sit entirely in the minority of B that isn't C. Now check each choice: is it flawed, and is the flaw this one? Two choices are valid (A uses "every" for the middle link; D's two "most" claims are about the same group). The key states its "all" premise first, so read for structure, not order.

choices.note: Valid. Most A are B, and all B are C and all C are D, so the A's that are B are D. There's no most-most link, so there's no flaw to match.

Flawed, but differently. It infers that sight-readers who auditioned belong to the orchestra from the fact that all orchestra members are sight-readers, reversing an "every" statement, and it concludes "most" rather than "at least one."

CORRECT. Most seminar students (A) are club members (B); most club members (B) volunteered (C); all volunteers (C) have training (D); so some A is D. It fails exactly as the columnist's does: the seminar students could all be among the club members who never volunteered. Only the order of the premises differs.

The tempting look-alike, but valid. Both "most" statements are about the same group, Larch Street residents, so more than half own cars and more than half signed. The two groups must overlap, and anyone in the overlap is invited.

Same premises, wrong conclusion. It concludes about the trails NOT open to cyclists, which the premises say nothing about. It is a different error from drawing a conclusion about A through a most-most chain.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Over the past decade, marsh frog populations in the lake district have fallen sharply, and the usual explanation is a fungal infection that spread through the region during that time. But the fungus cannot be the principal cause. A survey of twelve lakes found the fungus in frogs at every one of them, yet at four of those lakes frog populations have remained stable or even grown. Whatever principally drove the declines at the other eight lakes, then, must be something that is present at those eight but either absent or much weaker at the four. Since the fungus is present at all twelve lakes, it does not fit that description, and researchers would do better to look for a cause among the other differences between the two groups of lakes, such as water temperature or the presence of introduced fish.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the ecologist's argument depends?
choices: The fungus is not substantially less widespread or less damaging among the frogs at the four stable lakes than among the frogs at the other eight.
The fungus is equally widespread and equally damaging among the frogs at each of the twelve lakes surveyed.
Some factor present at the eight lakes with declining populations is entirely absent from all four of the lakes where frog populations have remained stable or have grown.
Frog populations at the four stable lakes were not larger than those at the other eight before the fungus spread through the region.
If the fungus had never reached a given lake, frog populations at that lake would not have declined.
questions.explanation: The ecologist's own test is that the cause must be absent or much weaker at the four stable lakes. Showing the fungus is present at all twelve rules out "absent" but not "much weaker." The argument needs the fungus not to be much weaker at the four, (A). (B) would close the gap, but it is too strong: the fungus could vary a little across lakes and the argument would still stand.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The fungus is not the principal cause of the frog declines.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The principal cause must be present at the eight declining lakes but absent or much weaker at the four stable ones; the fungus is present at all twelve.

breakdown.analysis: The ecologist sets a two-part test ("absent or much weaker") and then checks only the first part ("present at all twelve"). Presence is not strength. If the fungus infected only a few frogs, or a milder strain, at the four stable lakes, it would fit the ecologist's description perfectly. So the argument requires that it not be much weaker there. Expect the tempting answer to be the strong version, "the same everywhere". Negate it and see whether the argument actually dies.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the half of the ecologist's own test that the evidence never checks.
choices.negation: The fungus IS substantially less widespread or less damaging at the four stable lakes. Then it is "much weaker" there and fits the ecologist's description of the cause. The argument collapses.

choices.note: The trap. It would make the argument work, but it isn't required. Small differences between lakes don't matter; only a substantial weakening at the four would.
choices.negation: The fungus is not equally widespread and damaging at all twelve lakes; say it's slightly more common at some. If it is not much weaker at the four, the argument survives.

choices.note: The ecologist allows that the real cause may be merely "much weaker" at the four lakes, so it doesn't need to be entirely absent from them.
choices.negation: No factor at the eight is entirely absent from the four. A factor could still be much weaker there, and the ecologist explicitly allows that. Survives.

choices.note: Starting sizes don't bear on whether the fungus fits the ecologist's test, which is about the trend at each lake.
choices.negation: The stable lakes had larger populations to begin with. That doesn't make the fungus weaker there. Survives.

choices.note: This is irrelevant to whether the fungus is the principal cause. If anything, it suggests the fungus does matter.
choices.negation: Even without the fungus, populations at some lake would have declined. That's consistent with, even supportive of, the fungus not being the principal cause. Survives.
